items.title: Aurelius Atlas
items.text:
Data governance made simple. Aurelius Atlas is an open-source data governance solution that enables business users to find, understand, and trust their data without waiting on IT: discover data assets and their context in seconds, see who is accountable for them and whether they are fit for purpose, follow the journey and transformations of data across systems, and keep sensitive information in line with regulations such as GDPR.

It is one all-in-one data catalogue, designed to be business-user-friendly, meeting the demands of modern distributed data environments.

This repository builds the new engine behind that product: a Python re-implementation of Apache Atlas that keeps the Atlas 2.4.0 REST API and the Atlas dashboard, with Elasticsearch 9 as the only backend instead of JanusGraph, HBase and Solr — so the catalogue is far easier to run and cheaper to operate. The original Java Atlas is converted in small, reviewed increments, each proven against the Atlas 2.4.0 source code, so the clients, integrations, and dashboards organisations rely on keep working exactly as they do today.

Start with the User Guide for what the catalogue does for your organisation, the Conversion roadmap for plan and status, the Architecture overview for the system as it will stand, and the Contributor Guide to set up your machine.

The User Guide is intentionally short: until the conversion is complete, the Apache Atlas documentation describes the behaviour this system reproduces, and every intended difference is listed in Deviations from Apache Atlas.

items.title: About the team
items.text: This project is maintained by the Aurelius Enterprise team. Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions, need assistance, or would like to contribute.

items.title: API Reference
items.text:
Generated API documentation for the Aurelius Atlas workspace, rendered from the docstrings in each project by mkdocstrings. The prose for what a project is lives in its README.md; the wiring for how it is built and run lives in its AGENTS.md (ADR 003). This tree is the reference for what it exposes: classes, functions, signatures, and examples.

Each page doubles as that component's design documentation: the technology-specific detail of how the component works — settings and knob names, storage layout, protocol mechanics, ports, commands. The architecture trees state the technology-neutral properties the component must keep. A page's Design section carries this detail, with the ADR that owns each rule linked.

  • Apps — the services: the Atlas server and the template examples
  • Libs — the Python, Angular, and style libraries the apps consume

items.title: Apps
items.text: API reference for the workspace applications. The Atlas product is aurelius-atlas-server; the FastAPI and Angular examples are the template's demonstrations, kept until the conversion plan is done (DD-019) and then removed (ADR 050).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example
items.text: This is an example FastAPI application.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Run the following command to start the application locally:

python -m aurelius_atlas_fastapi_example

This launches a Uvicorn server at http://127.0.0.1:8000.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy using the provided Dockerfile. By default, the app listens on http://0.0.0.0:8000.

items.title: enforce_auth_security pydantic-validator
items.text:
enforce_auth_security() -> Settings

Fail fast when a non-development deployment misconfigures authentication or authorization.

Two silent-downgrade paths are closed here:

  • A plaintext auth_server_url lets a network-path attacker serve a forged OpenID configuration / JWKS, which mints tokens this API would accept — the whole bearer-token scheme collapses. OAuth token endpoints elsewhere in the workspace are https-only for the same reason.
  • An empty auth_audience (no AUTH_CLIENT_ID, no explicit audience) would accept any token from the issuer, and an empty auth_write_role would authenticate every caller for mutating operations. Both must be explicit.

items.title: enforce_transport_security pydantic-validator
items.text:
enforce_transport_security() -> Settings

Fail fast when a non-development deployment runs with unverified transport.

The defaults (database_sslmode="prefer", empty tls_cert_file) are convenient for local development, where the TLS material lives in the project .env. Outside development they must be set explicitly: otherwise a deployment that forgets the variables silently downgrades to opportunistic/unverified TLS — credentials and tokens over a channel a network-path attacker can read or impersonate.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-frontend-example
items.text: This is an example frontend application built with Angular.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy using the provided Dockerfile. By default, the app listens on http://localhost:8080.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: The following configuration is required to run the application:

items.title: Client-Facing Configuration
items.text:
The application is configured at runtime via an externally mounted config.json file. This client-facing configuration file contains the necessary settings for the frontend to communicate with the backend and authentication services. Below is an example config.json file:

{
    "keycloak": {
        "clientId": "aurelius",
        "realm": "master",
        "url": "http://keycloak.localhost:8181"
    }
}

Mount the config.json file into the container at /usr/share/nginx/html/config.json via a Docker volume or Docker configs mechanism.

items.title: Nginx Configuration
items.text:
The production image already bundles the locale-aware Nginx configuration for the Angular app. The bundled file is served at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf, and optional fragments may be added under /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf inside the existing server block.

The image serves locale-prefixed routes (/en-US/, /nl-NL/), redirects / to the preferred language, and falls back to the matching locale's index.html for client-side routing. Keep the app-serving rules in the image and add only server-scoped proxy or TLS fragments via /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf.

server {
    listen 8080;
    root /usr/share/nginx/html;

    include /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf;

    set $accept_language en-US;
    location = / {
        if ($http_accept_language ~* "^nl") {
            set $accept_language nl-NL;
        }
        return 302 /$accept_language/$is_args$args;
    }

    location /en-US/ {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /en-US/index.html;
    }

    location /nl-NL/ {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /nl-NL/index.html;
    }

    location / {
        try_files $uri /en-US/index.html;
    }
}

Do not define another server block or an HTTP-level map in a fragment; the hardened image includes fragments at server scope only.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-server
items.text: The Aurelius Atlas server: the Apache Atlas 2.4.0 REST API on Elasticsearch.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
npx nx serve aurelius-atlas-server

This starts the dev Elasticsearch store and the observability stack, then the server at https://localhost:21000, the port Apache Atlas uses.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy the image built from the provided Dockerfile. It listens on port 21000 and needs the Elasticsearch settings; it does not start without its store.

items.title: Design
items.text:
The technology-specific detail of how the server runs. The properties it must keep are in the architecture: Configuration Management (ADR 018), Components & Interfaces.

Settings. Read once at start-up into a frozen ServerSettings; a validation failure (missing key, bad scheme, half a TLS pair) stops start-up with a message naming the variable (SRV-01, SRV-02). All names carry the AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_ prefix. What a deployment must supply, with no defaults:

Variable Purpose ..._ELASTICSEARCH_HOSTS JSON list of store node URLs, e.g. ["https://es-0:9200"] — https only ..._ELASTICSEARCH_PASSWORD Store password — a SecretStr, never shown in logs ..._ELASTICSEARCH_CA_CERTS PEM CA of the store certificate; the store link is https-only (ADR 039) ..._TLS_CERT_FILE + ..._TLS_KEY_FILE PEM pair for serving HTTPS: both set, or both unset — enforced at start-up

With defaults: HOST (0.0.0.0 in the image), PORT (21000, Atlas's port — kept so existing clients find the catalogue where Atlas was, ADR 046), LOG_LEVEL, REVISION (reported by admin/version, ADM-01), DASHBOARD_DIR (None serves the API only, DSH-04), MODELS_DIR (default: the vendored Atlas 2.4.0 addons/models, MDL-16/DD-032), TYPEDEF_REFRESH_SECONDS (5.0 — how long the server answers from its type registry before checking for another process's type change, TDS-13/DD-029).

A half TLS pair stops the server from starting

TLS_CERT_FILE and TLS_KEY_FILE are both set, or both unset — the pairing is enforced at start-up. A container that mounts only the certificate exits with a message naming the missing variable; this is the design working, not a broken image.

The image (apps/aurelius-atlas-server/Dockerfile: hardened base, runs as nonroot) bakes in the production defaults — listen on 0.0.0.0:21000, dashboards served from /application/dashboard — and a liveness healthcheck against /api/atlas/admin/liveness that verifies the server's own certificate when TLS is on. Liveness is the probe a restart decision uses; readiness also fails while the store is away (DD-016).

Parity scenarios. scenarios/<resource>/*.scenario.yaml state each expectation as Atlas's own answer — e.g. scenarios/admin/version.scenario.yaml expects Version: "2.4.0", Name: apache-atlas, the exact content type — each cited to the Java source that produces it. Build-varying fields are marked volatile; the two places Aurelius Atlas must answer differently (name, description) carry a deviations: DV-03 entry. Anything else that differs fails the scenario (ADR 052).

items.title: aurelius_atlas_auth.auth
items.text:
Keycloak bearer-token authentication for Aurelius Atlas services (8.0, DD-197).

Ported from the template's FastAPI example (the workspace's reference for the pattern: apps/aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example/.../providers/auth.py), reshaped as a per-service object so each application owns one :class:KeycloakAuth built from its own settings — no module-level caches shared across applications.

The verification story (AUX-02..AUX-05):

  • OIDC discovery and JWKS are fetched through a circuit breaker (a Keycloak outage is a 503, not a hang) and cached for an hour.
  • Tokens are verified with PyJWT by kid: RS256 signature, issuer and expiry. The audience is checked after decoding against the union of the azp and aud claims, which pyjwt's built-in check cannot express.
  • The write gate accepts the configured role from realm_access.roles or resource_access.<audience>.roles — Keycloak namespaces client roles per client, so only this service's own client entry counts.

  • AuthConfig –

    What a service needs to verify its tokens. Apps map their settings in.

  • KeycloakAuth –

    One service's Keycloak verifier: dependencies for FastAPI routers.

  • bearer_scheme –

    The scheme every :class:KeycloakAuth shares: one instance keeps FastAPI's

items.title: aurelius-atlas-core
items.text:
Atlas stores and services for Aurelius Atlas (DD-002). Since increment 1.4: the typedef store, which keeps type definitions in one Elasticsearch document and serves them from the type registry. Since 1.5: Apache Atlas's built-in models and their typedef patches, loaded at start-up. Since 1.6: the store's reads and the search of /v2/types/typedefs. Since 2.2: the entity store, which keeps each entity as one Elasticsearch document, reserves unique attribute values and writes several entities all or nothing through a journal (DD-043 to DD-048).

store = TypedefStore(TypeRegistry(), ElasticsearchTypedefDocument(elasticsearch_store.client))
await store.load()  # every stored definition into the registry
created = await store.create_types_def(types_def)
await store.refresh()  # pick up another process's change (at most every 5 s)
await ModelLoader(store).load(BUILTIN_MODELS_DIR)  # addons/models of Atlas 2.4.0, and their patches
store.get_by_name("hive_table")  # the registered definition, as resolution completed it
search_types_def(store.registry, TypeSearchFilter.from_query([("type", "ENTITY")]))  # each kind sorted by name

items.title: Installation
items.text:
dependencies = ["aurelius-atlas-core"]

[tool.uv.sources.aurelius-atlas-core]
workspace = true

items.title: Vendored models
items.text:
aurelius_atlas_core/models/ is addons/models of Apache Atlas release-2.4.0, byte for byte (DD-032). To prove it, compare it with the tag:

diff -r <apache-atlas checkout at release-2.4.0>/addons/models libs/python/aurelius-atlas-core/aurelius_atlas_core/models

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.typedef_store
items.text:
The typedef store: type definitions kept in Elasticsearch and served from the registry (TDS-01 to TDS-13).

Ported from AtlasTypeDefGraphStore and its def stores (Atlas*DefStoreV2) of Apache Atlas 2.4.0. A change is tried on the registry's transient copy, checked as Atlas's def stores check it, written as one document (DD-028) and only then committed to the registry (TDS-10). The document also holds the record of each typedef patch, written with the patch's change (DD-031).

Type Aliases:

  • TypeUsage –

    Whether entities, classifications or relationships of a type exist (DD-030).

Classes:

  • PatchChange –

    What a typedef patch decided (MDL-07): its status, and the definitions it updates, if any.

  • TypedefStore –

    Type definitions kept in a TypedefDocument, served from a TypeRegistry (AtlasTypeDefGraphStore).

Functions:

  • is_newer_version –

    ObjectUtils.compare(new, old) > 0: compared as strings, an absent version less than any (MDL-02).

  • is_valid_name –

    A letter, then letters, digits, spaces or _; optionally after __ (isValidName, TDS-02).

  • java_compare –

    Compare as Java's String.compareTo does: by UTF-16 code unit (MDL-01, MDL-02).

  • never_in_use –

    The type usage until the entity store exists (2.2): no type is in use (DD-030).

  • rectify –

    Repair what older stores allowed, as rectifyTypeErrorsIfAny does on load (TDS-12).

  • referenced_type_names –

    The type names inside array<…> and map<…,…> (AtlasTypeUtil.getReferencedTypeNames, TDS-04).

  • types_def_of –

    An AtlasTypesDef holding typedefs, each in the list of its kind.

  • types_to_create –

    The definitions whose name is not registered, as any kind or built-in (getTypesToCreate, MDL-02).

  • types_to_update –

    The definitions registered as the same kind, when newer (getTypesToUpdate, MDL-02).

Attributes:

  • ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE –

    The patch action under which an update may add mandatory attributes (TYPEDEF_PATCH_ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE).

  • DEFAULT_REFRESH_SECONDS –

    How long a process answers from its registry before it checks for another process's change (DD-029).

items.title: apply_patch async
items.text:
apply_patch(patch: AtlasPatch, decide: Callable[[TypeRegistry], PatchChange]) -> PatchStatus | None

Apply a typedef patch unless its record says it is done, and record how it ended (MDL-05, MDL-06).

decide looks at the registry and says what the patch does; an AtlasError from it, or from the update it asks for, makes the patch FAILED, and leaves the definitions as they were. Any other error is raised. The patch's record is written with its change (DD-031); a patch without an id is not recorded.

Returns:

  • PatchStatus | None –

    How the patch ended, or None when its record says it was applied or skipped before.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.entity_store
items.text:
EntityStore: entities by GUID and unique attributes, written all or nothing (ENS-02 to ENS-09).

The storage side of AtlasEntityStoreV2 and EntityGraphMapper: what a graph transaction gave Atlas, rebuilt on Elasticsearch with reserved unique values, conditional writes and a journal (DD-044 to DD-048).

Classes:

  • ClassificationChange –

    One classification instance of a write: its new state and the version it was read in, or None for a new one.

  • EntityChange –

    One entity of a write: its new state, and the version it was read in, or None for a new entity.

  • EntityStore –

    Entities of the registry's entity types, and the relationships between them, in EntityDocuments.

  • EntityVersionConflictError –

    Another write changed an entity after it was read (ENS-08); nothing was written.

  • EntityWriteError –

    An entity could not be written for another reason; the write was undone (ENS-07).

  • RelationshipChange –

    One relationship of a write: its new state and the version it was read in, or None for a new one.

  • TaskChange –

    One task of a write: its new state and the version it was read in, or None for a new one (DD-079).

  • UniqueValueTakenError –

    A write needs a unique value another entity holds (ENS-05); nothing was written.

Attributes:

  • LEASE_MILLISECONDS –

    How long a write may take before recovery may undo it (DD-046).

  • LEASE_PASSED_ERROR –
  • REMOVE_UNREAD_ERROR –
  • UNIQUE_VALUE_TAKEN_ERROR –
  • UNKNOWN_ENTITY_TYPE_ERROR –
  • VERSION_CONFLICT_ERROR –
  • WRITE_FAILED_ERROR –

items.text:
The entities' documents in Elasticsearch: entities, unique value reservations and the write journal (ENS-01).

The I/O behind EntityStore: reads in real time, conditional writes, create-only reservations (DD-043 to DD-047). Documents go to Elasticsearch as the bytes of Atlas's JSON codec, so values keep their digits (DD-039).

Type Aliases:

  • Linked –

    A document an entity lists: a relationship or a classification instance.

Classes:

  • ElasticsearchEntityDocuments –

    EntityDocuments in three Elasticsearch indices behind aliases (DD-043, DD-045, DD-046).

  • EntityDocuments –

    Where EntityStore keeps entities, reservations and its journal.

  • JournalEntry –

    A write in flight: its id, lease, the entities' states before it, its reservations, releases and removals.

  • LinkedKind –

    The documents an entity lists besides itself, each in an index of its own (DD-061, DD-070).

  • LinkedWrite –

    What a write does to the documents of one LinkedKind: written ones at a version or new, removed ones.

  • Reservation –

    A unique value held by an entity: the key's id, the holder's GUID and the write that reserved it (DD-045).

  • VersionedClassification –

    A stored classification instance and the version it was read in (DD-047, DD-070).

  • VersionedEntity –

    A stored entity and the version it was read in (DD-047).

  • VersionedRelationship –

    A stored relationship and the version it was read in (DD-047, DD-061).

  • WriteResult –

    How one entity of a bulk write ended: written, or failed by a version conflict or another error.

Attributes:

  • CLASSIFICATION_INDEX –

    The alias of the classification index (DD-070).

  • CLASSIFICATION_MAPPING (dict[str, Any]) –

    Classification instances by type and entity; attribute values stored, not indexed (DD-070).

  • CLASSIFICATION_PAGE –

    How many classification instances one search page holds.

  • ENTITY_FIELD_LIMIT –

    index.mapping.total_fields.limit of the entity index: a field per searchable attribute (DD-088).

  • ENTITY_INDEX –

    The alias of the entity index (DD-043).

  • ENTITY_MAPPING (dict[str, Any]) –

    System properties and referenced GUIDs mapped for exact lookup; attribute values stored, not indexed, and searched

  • INDEX_PREFIX –

    The prefix of the three aliases; tests give their own.

  • JOURNAL_INDEX –

    The alias of the write journal (DD-046).

  • JOURNAL_PAGE –

    How many journal entries recovery reads at once; a live journal holds one entry per write in flight.

  • KEYWORD_LIMIT –

    ignore_above of keyword search fields: the longest value a keyword holds, in characters (DD-092).

  • LINKED_MODELS (dict[LinkedKind, type[StoredRelationship | StoredClassification | StoredTask]]) –
  • REFERRING_PAGE –

    How many referring entities one search page holds (DD-057).

  • RELATIONSHIP_INDEX –

    The alias of the relationship index (DD-061).

  • RELATIONSHIP_MAPPING (dict[str, Any]) –

    Relationships by type, label, ends and state; attribute values stored, not indexed (DD-061).

  • TASK_MAPPING (dict[str, Any]) –

    Tasks by status and creation time; parameters stored, not indexed (DD-079).

  • TASK_PAGE –

    How many tasks one search page holds.

  • UNIQUE_VALUE_INDEX –

    The alias of the unique value reservations (DD-045).

items.title: ElasticsearchEntityDocuments
items.text:
ElasticsearchEntityDocuments(client: AsyncElasticsearch, prefix: str = INDEX_PREFIX)

EntityDocuments in three Elasticsearch indices behind aliases (DD-043, DD-045, DD-046).

Methods:

  • classifications_of_types –

    Refresh the classification index, then page through the instances of the types by GUID (DD-090).

  • classified –

    Refresh the entity index, then page through the entities whose classificationGuids hold one (DD-076).

  • count_linked_type –

    Refresh the kind's index, then count its documents of the type (REL-10, CLS-12).

  • count_type –

    Refresh the entity index, then count the entities of the type (DD-048).

  • delete_journal –

    Delete the entry; one already gone is fine.

  • get –

    mget of the entity index: real time, as a get by id is (ENS-04).

  • get_linked –

    mget of the kind's index: real time (DD-061, DD-070).

  • journal –

    The entries of the journal, refreshed first so none written a moment ago is missed.

  • list_tasks –

    Refresh the task index, then page through its tasks by creation time (TSK-04, TSK-06).

  • prepare –

    Create each index behind its alias unless it exists (ENS-01).

  • put_journal –

    Index the entry under its write id.

  • referring –

    Refresh the entity index, then page through the entities whose references hold a GUID (DD-057).

  • release –

    Delete the reservation when guid still holds it, guarded by its version.

  • reservations –

    mget of the reservations, in real time.

  • reserve –

    op_type=create: of two processes reserving one value, one fails (DD-045).

  • restore –

    Index the state before, or delete an entity that did not exist before (DD-046).

  • restore_linked –

    Index the document's state before, or delete one that did not exist before (DD-062).

  • search –

    Refresh the entity index, then answer the query as a bool query of the search fields (DD-089).

  • write –

    One bulk request over the indices: create a new document, index or delete with if_seq_no.

Attributes:

  • aliases (tuple[str, ...]) –

    The aliases of the entity index, the reservations, the journal and the linked documents' indices.

items.title: EntityDocuments
items.text:
Bases: Protocol

Where EntityStore keeps entities, reservations and its journal.

Methods:

  • classifications_of_types –

    The classification instances of these types, or of every type for None, as of now (DD-090).

  • classified –

    The entities listing any of these classification instances, as of now (DD-076).

  • count_linked_type –

    How many documents of the kind and type exist, in any state, as of now (REL-10, CLS-12).

  • count_type –

    How many entities of exactly this type exist, in any state, as of now.

  • delete_journal –

    Delete a journal entry.

  • get –

    The stored entities with these GUIDs, in real time; unknown GUIDs are left out.

  • get_linked –

    The stored documents of a kind with these GUIDs, in real time; unknown GUIDs are left out (DD-061).

  • journal –

    Every journal entry.

  • list_tasks –

    Every task, or those PENDING or IN_PROGRESS, oldest first, as of now (TSK-04, TSK-06).

  • prepare –

    Create the indices that are missing.

  • put_journal –

    Write a journal entry.

  • referring –

    The entities whose references name any of these GUIDs, as of now (DD-057).

  • release –

    Delete the reservation of key if guid holds it.

  • reservations –

    The reservations of these keys that exist.

  • reserve –

    Make a reservation, create-only; the one holding the key when it is taken.

  • restore –

    Put back an entity's state before a write, or delete one the write created.

  • restore_linked –

    Put back a linked document's state before a write, or delete one the write created (DD-062).

  • search –

    The entities of the query's page, as of now, how many match it in all, and their scores (DD-089).

  • write –

    Write and remove entities and linked documents, new (no version) or at the version given.

items.text:
StoredEntity: an entity as stored, its system properties and its attribute values (ENS-03, DD-043).

What EntityGraphMapper and GraphHelper keep on an entity's vertex: the GUID, type and super type names, state, times, users, version and the attribute values, here under their qualified names.

Classes:

  • StoredEntity –

    One document of the entity index; write_id names the write that last wrote it (DD-046).

Functions:

  • stored_attributes –

    Attribute values keyed by qualified name; names the type does not have are left out (DD-043).

items.title: StoredEntity
items.text:
Bases: AtlasModel

One document of the entity index; write_id names the write that last wrote it (DD-046).

Methods:

  • listing –

    This entity listing relationship relationship_guid as one it is an end of (DD-061).

items.text: The contract and the async client of the data2model extraction API (8.4, DD-203, DD-204): the rules family the legacy chain evolved (AURELIUS-RULES), the extraction request/response, and the Data2ModelClient that posts them. The aurelius-atlas-data2model app imports its own contract from here.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_data2model_client.models
items.text:
The /extract request contract as pydantic models (DTM-01, DTM-11, DTM-12; DD-198).

The legacy chain built these from m4i-analytics dict adapters (ConceptDefinition and subclasses, **kwargs-tolerant); the port states the same fields as pydantic models, so FastAPI validates the public request at the boundary: an unknown concept or relationship type, a missing required key, or a dangling rule reference is a 400 (DTM-11), not a 500 as in the legacy.

The legacy adapters normalise None prefixes/keys to '' — the lineage caller sends nulls for them — so the string fields accept None and normalise to ''; extra keys (alias, description, include, …) are ignored, as the **kwargs did. The tabular data stays a plain list of row maps: the columns are the rules' keys, so the rows are a mapping, not a model (DD-198).

Classes:

  • ElementRule –

    An element rule (legacy ElementDefinition): one node per row of id_key.

  • ExtractionRequest –

    The POST /extract body: {data: [row…], rules: {...}}.

  • ExtractionResponse –

    The POST /extract answer: {metadata: […], model: "<ar3 JSON string>"}.

  • MappingEntry –

    One {key, value}: attach column value as metadata attribute key.

  • MetadataEntry –

    One {id, data} metadata entry of the extraction answer.

  • RelationRule –

    A relation rule (legacy RelationshipDefinition): one edge per row.

  • RulesDef –

    The rules body: elements, relations, views, in rule order.

  • ViewEdgeRule –

    A view edge entry: includes the referenced relation rule's edges.

  • ViewNodeRule –

    A view node entry: includes the referenced element rule's nodes.

  • ViewRule –

    A view rule (legacy ViewDefinition): one diagram per layout match.

Attributes:

  • LegacyStr –

    A legacy string field: null arrives as '', as the legacy adapters normalise it.

  • UNKNOWN_CONCEPT_TYPE_ERROR –

    A concept_type outside the ported type table (DTM-11).

  • UNKNOWN_ELEMENT_RULE_ERROR –

    A relation rule's dangling source/target reference (DTM-11).

  • UNKNOWN_RELATIONSHIP_TYPE_ERROR –

    A relationship_type outside the ported shorthand table (DTM-11).

  • UNKNOWN_VIEW_EDGE_RULE_ERROR –

    A view rule's dangling view_edges reference (DTM-11).

  • UNKNOWN_VIEW_NODE_RULE_ERROR –

    A view rule's dangling view_nodes reference (DTM-11).

items.title: aurelius_atlas_data2model_client.client
items.text:
The async client for the data2model API (CL-01..CL-05, CL-21; DD-203, DD-204, DD-205).

The shared client conventions of increment 8.4: constructed from an externally built httpx.AsyncClient and a token source, reading no environment variables (CL-01) — the app builds the httpx client from its own settings and passes it in. The request path is relative, appended to that client's base URL, so a URL with a trailing slash — the str() of a pydantic HttpUrl — works as given (CL-01); the builder closes the pool, the API client never touches its lifecycle. Tests hand over one built on a MockTransport and no socket opens (CL-02); the bearer token goes on every call (CL-03); :class:Data2ModelClientError rises on a non-2xx answer, with the Atlas-shaped body when it parses (CL-04); an unreachable upstream propagates as httpx's own error (CL-05).

extract posts an :class:~aurelius_atlas_data2model_client.models.ExtractionRequest — the same model class the server validates — and returns an :class:~aurelius_atlas_data2model_client.models.ExtractionResponse, so the 8.2 chain's payload and the 8.1 answer are one contract on both sides (CL-21).

Type Aliases:

  • TokenSource –

    Where the bearer token comes from: a fixed token, or a callable that yields one (CL-03).

Classes:

    The client for one data2model service (CL-21, DD-203, DD-205).

  • Data2ModelClientError –

    A non-2xx answer from the data2model API, with the status and the error body (CL-04).

Attributes:

  • CLIENT_ERROR –

    The status where an answer becomes an error: the client-error boundary (CL-04).

  • DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS –

    The suggested request timeout, seconds — for the httpx client an app builds (DD-200's bound).

  • EXTRACT_PATH –

    The extraction endpoint of the data2model app (DTM-01), relative to the base URL (CL-01).

items.title: avro_schema classmethod
items.text:
avro_schema(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any]

Return the Avro schema with datetime fields encoded as timestamp-millis.

pydantic-avro defaults date-time fields to timestamp-micros, but the Confluent Avro converter maps only timestamp-millis to the Connect Timestamp logical type. Without it, consumers that read through that converter (e.g. the Debezium JDBC sink) see a nameless raw INT64 and try to bind it to a timestamptz column as a bigint, which fails.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client.models
items.text:
The request and response shapes of the lineage-model API (CL-30, LM-01/LM-04; DD-203).

The ids of this module's rules stay here: LineageModelParams is LM-01's query (DV-72/DV-73 are its rejections), LineageModelResponse is the LM-04/LM-01 forward of the data2model answer (DV-68's contract). Field descriptions are the public OpenAPI documentation, so they name no rule ids; the Java classes ported are in the increment spec.

The query of GET / and the answer it forwards from data2model, stated once so the app validates its own query with the same model a caller builds (CL-07). The lineage directions are imported from aurelius-atlas-server-client — the lineage vocabulary belongs to the lineage API (CL-12), not to each consumer; reusing it is CL-10's rule applied to types.

Classes:

  • LineageModelParams –

    The GET / query of the lineage-model API: which entity, how deep, which way.

  • LineageModelResponse –

    The answer of GET /: the flattened lineage as an ar3 model and its metadata.

Attributes:

  • DEFAULT_DEPTH –

    The lineage depth the endpoint defaults to when the query omits it (LM-01).

  • MIN_DEPTH –

items.title: aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client.client
items.text:
The async client for the lineage-model API (CL-01..CL-05, CL-30; DD-203, DD-204, DD-205).

The shared client conventions of increment 8.4: constructed from an externally built httpx.AsyncClient and a token source, reading no environment variables (CL-01). The request path is relative, appended to that client's base URL, so a URL with a trailing slash — the str() of a pydantic HttpUrl — works as given (CL-01); the builder closes the pool, the API client never touches its lifecycle. Tests hand over one built on a MockTransport and no socket opens (CL-02); the bearer goes on every call (CL-03); LineageModelClientError rises on a non-2xx answer with the Atlas-shaped body when it parses (CL-04); an unreachable upstream propagates as httpx's own error (CL-05).

The 204 of LM-05/LM-06 — the empty answer, no model — is not an error: it maps to None, the caller's success path (CL-04).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-model
items.text:
Atlas data shapes for Aurelius Atlas, without I/O (DD-002). Since increment 1.1: the Apache Atlas 2.4.0 type definitions (enum, struct, classification, entity, relationship and business metadata), their header and AtlasTypesDef, as Pydantic models that read and write Atlas's REST JSON. Since 1.5: the patch record AtlasPatch. Since 2.1a: the entity models of aurelius_atlas_model.instance, one module per Atlas class (AtlasEntity, AtlasEntityWithExtInfo, AtlasEntityHeader, AtlasClassification, AtlasObjectId, EntityMutationResponse, …), and the JSON conventions all models share in aurelius_atlas_model.base. Since 2.1b: Atlas's JSON codec, aurelius_atlas_model.codec, which keeps the digits of decimals.

from aurelius_atlas_model.typedef import AtlasTypesDef

types = AtlasTypesDef.model_validate(request_body)  # Atlas's normalisations apply
response_body = types.to_json()  # Java names, nulls left out, epoch-millisecond dates

from aurelius_atlas_model.instance import AtlasEntitiesWithExtInfo

entities = AtlasEntitiesWithExtInfo.model_validate(request_body)  # entities without a GUID get "-<n>"

Atlas type definitions as Pydantic models that read and write Atlas's REST JSON (DD-020).

Ported from org.apache.atlas.model.typedef of Apache Atlas 2.4.0. Field names are snake_case in Python and the Java getter names in JSON (TDM-01). The normalisations the Java setters and constructors apply run as validators, so they hold for request bodies and for models built in code alike.

The TDM-nn rule each class and field ports is cited in the increment spec, not in class docstrings or field descriptions: those are public and end up in the OpenAPI schema, where decision ids mean nothing to a client.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_model.codec
items.text:
Atlas's JSON: numbers with a fraction read as decimals, decimals and dates written as Jackson writes them.

Atlas's REST mapper reads floats as BigDecimal (USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS) and writes a BigDecimal with its digits and a Date as epoch milliseconds (VAL-01, DD-039).

Functions:

  • dumps –

    Write value as Atlas's REST mapper does, compactly, in UTF-8 (VAL-01).

  • loads –

    Read JSON as Jackson does with USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS: every float is a Decimal with its digits.

Attributes:

  • NOT_JSON_ERROR –

items.text:
dumps(value: Any) -> bytes

Write value as Atlas's REST mapper does, compactly, in UTF-8 (VAL-01).

A Decimal keeps its digits, a datetime is epoch milliseconds, NaN and infinities are strings, a model is its to_json, and map keys are Java's text of the key.

items.text: The OTLP ingest credential for the collector's per-service leg (7.18, DD-196), shared by every Aurelius Atlas service that exports telemetry with a Keycloak client-credentials identity (8.0, DD-197).

items.title: aurelius_atlas_otel.ingest
items.text:
The OTLP ingest credential for the collector's per-service leg (7.18, DD-196, CIA-07).

The collector's per-service leg (4317 gRPC / 4319 HTTP) accepts only Keycloak client-credentials JWTs minted for the service's realm client otel-<service> (audience otel-collector, the otel-ingest scope). The OTel Python SDK reads OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS statically, and the dev realm's access token lives 60s — a bearer JWT in a static header expires a minute in. So the app owns the OTLP export: a refresh-ahead token source feeds a requests.Session that injects a fresh bearer header on every OTLP request, handed to app-built exporters whose processor/reader setup_telemetry installs on the process's providers (DD-210).

Extracted from the Atlas server's otel_ingest module so every service on the leg shares one credential (8.0, DD-197); the server keeps the settings mapping, this library owns the mechanism.

No new dependency: the session rides the requests the OTLP exporter already uses, and the mint is stdlib urllib. The dev realm's 60s token is why the header is read per request, not once.

    Mints and caches a client-credentials JWT, refreshed ahead of expiry.

bearer() -> str | None

A valid bearer token, minting/refreshing as needed.

On mint failure with no usable token, None — the request then goes out header-less and the collector's 401 is the visible failure (DD-196: no silent fallback).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-parity
items.text: Parity scenarios for Aurelius Atlas: the scenario format, the runner and the comparison.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Part of the workspace dev group, which loads the pytest plugin into every test run.

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["aurelius-atlas-parity"]

[tool.uv.sources.aurelius-atlas-parity]
workspace = true

items.title: aurelius_atlas_parity
items.text:
Parity scenarios: requests with the responses Apache Atlas 2.4.0 gives, run against Aurelius Atlas (ADR 052).

Modules:

  • compare –

    The exact comparison of a response body with its expectation (SCN-09, SCN-10, SCN-12; DD-013).

  • path –

    Paths into a JSON document: the JSONPath subset $, .name, ['name'], [n] and [*] (SCN-07).

  • plugin –

    The pytest plugin: gives each scenario test its endpoints and deviations as test properties (SCN-14; DD-014).

  • run –

    Running a scenario: send each stage's request, compare its response, save values (SCN-05 to SCN-12).

  • scenario –

    The scenario format: *.scenario.yaml files, read and validated (SCN-01 to SCN-03; DD-012).

  • testing –

    A sample ASGI application for this library's own tests.

Classes:

  • Scenario –

    One scenario file (SCN-01).

  • ScenarioError –

    A scenario file does not parse or does not match the format (SCN-03).

  • ScenarioFailedError –

    A stage's response differs from its expectation; the message lists every difference (SCN-11).

Functions:

  • load_scenarios –

    Read every *.scenario.yaml below a directory as pytest parameters, one test per scenario (SCN-04).

  • run_scenario –

    Run a scenario's stages in order through the client (SCN-05); {run} is unique to the run (SCN-16).

items.title: aurelius_atlas_parity.run
items.text:
Running a scenario: send each stage's request, compare its response, save values (SCN-05 to SCN-12).

Classes:

  • ScenarioFailedError –

    A stage's response differs from its expectation; the message lists every difference (SCN-11).

Functions:

  • check_response –

    Compare a response with a stage's expectation and return every difference (SCN-08 to SCN-12).

  • load_scenarios –

    Read every *.scenario.yaml below a directory as pytest parameters, one test per scenario (SCN-04).

  • run_scenario –

    Run a scenario's stages in order through the client (SCN-05); {run} is unique to the run (SCN-16).

  • substitute –

    Replace {name} by saved values in every string of a JSON value (SCN-06).

Attributes:

  • FAILURE_HEADER –
  • NOT_JSON_ERROR –
  • NO_DIRECTORY_ERROR –
  • RUN –

    The name every scenario run starts with: a value unique to the run, in letters and digits (SCN-16, DD-055).

  • SAVE_NOT_ONE_ERROR –
  • UNKNOWN_NAME_ERROR –

items.title: substitute
items.text:
substitute(value: Any, saved: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Any

Replace {name} by saved values in every string of a JSON value (SCN-06).

A string that is exactly {name} becomes the saved value with its JSON type; elsewhere the value is written into the string. Object keys are strings, so a value written into one is its text. {{ and }} stand for literal braces.

Raises:

  • KeyError –

    A name was not saved by an earlier stage.

items.title: setup_logger
items.text:
setup_logger(level: int | str = INFO) -> None

Set up logging for the application with a standardized log output format.

This function configures the logging system to use the specified logging level, with a custom log format that includes the timestamp, log level, logger name, and log message. Log levels can be provided as either an integer or a string corresponding to standard logging levels.

  • CRITICAL
  • ERROR
  • WARNING
  • INFO
  • DEBUG

Parameters:

Examples:

Set up logging with the default level. This will log messages with a level of INFO and above.

>>> setup_logging()

Set up logging to show DEBUG-level messages (and above) by providing the logging level's integer value.

>>> setup_logging(logging.DEBUG)

Set up logging by specifying the logging level as a string. This is equivalent to the previous example.

>>> setup_logging("DEBUG")

TLS_POSTGRES_HOST = 'localhost'

Host test clients connect to.

The ephemeral certificates cover only loopback names and libpq verifies the host parameter against them, so clients connect to localhost through the published port rather than to get_container_host_ip() (a bridge/gateway address in some Docker setups). items.title: configure_tls_postgres
items.text:
configure_tls_postgres(container: PostgresContainer, certs: TlsCertificates) -> None

Configure a PostgreSQL test container to enforce TLS, mirroring dev/postgres.

Call before the container starts. The server comes up with ssl=on and a hostssl-only pg_hba.conf, so plaintext TCP connections are rejected server-side; clients connect with sslmode=verify-full against certs.ca_bundle_path (host: :data:TLS_POSTGRES_HOST).

The hardened image runs as a fixed non-root user that cannot read host-owned key material it does not own, so — like dev/postgres — the certificates are copied into the container filesystem with strict permissions before startup (Postgres also refuses world-readable keys).

items.title: tls_certificates
items.text:
tls_certificates(*, prefix: str = 'aurelius-tls', sans: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_TLS_SANS) -> Generator[TlsCertificates]

Generate ephemeral TLS material, removing the directory again on exit.

A throwaway CA and server certificate (SANs: sans) live in a temporary directory - named with prefix - for the duration of the block, keeping the fixture as hermetic as the random credentials next to it; no certgen/decrypt is needed to run tests.

Parameters:

Usage in a fixture::

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def db_tls_material() -> Generator[TlsCertificates]:
    with tls_certificates() as certs:
        yield certs

items.title: aurelius_atlas_server_client.client
items.text:
The async client for the Atlas metadata API (CL-01..CL-05, CL-11; DD-203, DD-204, DD-205).

One client per server: constructed from an externally built httpx.AsyncClient and a token source, reading no environment variables (CL-01) — the app builds the httpx client from its own settings (TLS, timeout) and passes it in. The request paths are relative, appended to that client's base URL, so a URL with a trailing slash — the str() of a pydantic HttpUrl — works as given (CL-01); the builder closes the pool, the API client never touches its lifecycle. Because the client arrives from outside, tests hand over one built on a MockTransport and no socket opens (CL-02, the DD-200 seam made async). Every request carries authorization: Bearer <token> from the token source (CL-03); a non-2xx answer raises :class:AtlasClientError with the status and the server's {errorCode, errorMessage} when the body parses (CL-04); an unreachable upstream propagates as httpx's own error — mapping it to an HTTP status is the app's job (LM-07's DV-80), not the client's (CL-05).

The paths mirror the server's routes verbatim: routes/admin.py under /api/atlas/admin, routes/types.py under /api/atlas/v2/types, and the v2/lineage/{guid} feed of the server root (whose route lands with 5.1, CL-11).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-trace
items.text: Traceability for Aurelius Atlas: the covers marker, the coverage check and the test report.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Part of the workspace dev group, which loads the pytest plugin into every test run.

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["aurelius-atlas-trace"]

[tool.uv.sources.aurelius-atlas-trace]
workspace = true

items.title: aurelius_atlas_trace
items.text:
Modules:

  • check –

    The check: every public function and every rule is named by a test (ADR 049 R1, R2).

  • cli –

    The aurelius-atlas-trace command: check and report.

  • config –

    Which projects, packages and specifications the check covers (TRC-07), read from the root pyproject.toml.

  • report –

  • rules –

    The rules of the increment specifications: what R2 of ADR 049 says must be named by a test (TRC-08).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-typesystem
items.text:
The Atlas type system for Aurelius Atlas, without I/O (DD-002): the type registry and the types that type definitions resolve to. Since increment 1.2: the built-in, array, map, enum and struct types, attribute types and constraints. Since 1.3: entity and classification hierarchies, relationship and business metadata types. Since 2.1b: the value side of the built-in, enum, array and map types, as Atlas checks, normalises and compares attribute values. Since 2.1c: the same for structs, classifications (with their validity periods) and entities (with their relationship attributes).

from aurelius_atlas_typesystem.registry import TypeRegistry

registry = TypeRegistry()
with registry.update() as transient:  # committed when the block ends, discarded when it raises
    transient.add_types(types_def)  # resolves every type; raises AtlasError on a bad reference
registry.entity_type("hive_table")

int_type = registry.get_type("int")
int_type.get_normalized_value("42")  # 42; Java's Integer.valueOf rules, None when invalid
registry.get_type("array<int>").validate_value(["x"], "a", messages := [])  # messages: a[0]=x: invalid value…
registry.entity_type("hive_table").validate_value(entity, "entity", messages)  # e.g. mandatory attribute missing

dependencies = ["aurelius-atlas-typesystem"]

items.title: aurelius_atlas_typesystem.types
items.text:
Atlas types: the classes a type definition resolves to, one module per Java class (DD-025, DD-041).

This module re-exports them and makes the unresolved type of a definition (type_of).

Classes:

  • ArrayType –

    array<T> with its cardinality and value counts (AtlasArrayType, TRG-02).

  • AtlasAttribute –

    A resolved attribute of a struct-like type (AtlasStructType.AtlasAttribute).

  • AtlasType –

    A type: its name, category and service type, and how it checks, normalises and compares values.

  • BuiltInType –

    A primitive type such as string or int, of the atlas_core service type (TRG-01).

  • BusinessAttribute –

    A business metadata attribute and the entity types it applies to (AtlasBusinessAttribute, THY-12).

  • BusinessMetadataType –

    A business metadata type: its attributes and the entity types they apply to (THY-12).

  • ClassificationType –

    A classification type: its hierarchy and the entity types it applies to (THY-01 to THY-05, THY-07).

  • EdgeDirection –

    Which way a relationship attribute's edge points (AtlasRelationshipEdgeDirection, THY-10).

  • EntityType –

    An entity type: its hierarchy, relationship and business attributes (THY-01 to THY-06, THY-10 to THY-12).

  • EnumType –

    An enum type: its elements by value and ordinal, and its default (AtlasEnumType, TRG-14).

  • MapType –

    map<K,V> (AtlasMapType, TRG-02).

  • ObjectIdType –

    objectid: a reference to an entity of object_type, by GUID or by unique attributes.

  • RelationshipType –

    A relationship type: its ends, label and the attributes it adds to them (THY-08 to THY-10).

  • StructType –

    A struct type, and the base of every type with attributes (AtlasStructType, TRG-10 to TRG-13).

Functions:

  • entity_types_and_all_sub_types –

    The entity types named and all their sub types (getEntityTypesAndAllSubTypes, THY-07).

  • qualified_attribute_name –

    Type.attribute, or the name itself when it contains a dot or belongs to a root type (TRG-11, THY-05).

  • referenced_entity_type –

    The entity type a type, an array of it or a map to it refers to, or None (TRG-12).

  • type_of –

    The unresolved type of a definition, by its exact class (addTypeWithNoRefResolve).

  • validate_relationship_def –

    Check the ends' cardinality and containers against the category (validateAtlasRelationshipDef, THY-08).

A type: its name, category and service type, and how it checks, normalises and compares values.

The value methods are Java's, in snake_case: create_default_value is createDefaultValue, is_valid_value is isValidValue and so on. A value is a Java value as DD-040 holds it.

Methods:

  • are_equal_values –

    areEqualValues: both null, or both normalise to equal values (VAL-02).

  • create_default_value –

    The value an attribute of this type gets by default (createDefaultValue()).

  • create_default_value_of –

    createDefaultValue(Object): the default for null, else the normalised value (VAL-02).

  • create_optional_default_value –

    The default of an optional attribute; the default, unless a type says otherwise.

  • get_normalized_value –

    value as this type holds it, or None when it is not a value of this type (getNormalizedValue).

  • get_normalized_value_for_update –

    getNormalizedValueForUpdate: as get_normalized_value, unless a type says otherwise.

  • is_valid_value –

    Whether value is a value of this type (isValidValue).

  • is_valid_value_for_update –

    isValidValueForUpdate: as is_valid_value, unless a type says otherwise.

  • type_for_attribute –

    The type an attribute of this type holds; an entity type is held as an objectid (TRG-11).

  • validate_value –

    Whether value is valid; if not, add <name>=<value>: invalid value for type <type> (VAL-02).

  • validate_value_for_update –

    validateValueForUpdate: as validate_value, unless a type says otherwise.

Attributes:

  • category –
  • service_type –
  • type_name –

items.title: aurelius_atlas_typesystem.java
items.text:
Java's number conversions, on Java values held as Python values (DD-040).

A Java Integer, Long or BigInteger is an int, a BigDecimal a Decimal, a Double a float and a Float a float holding the shortest decimal of its 32-bit value. A bool is a Java Boolean, never a number. Each function is named after the Java method it ports.

  • JavaNumber –

items.text: The contract and the async client of the validate-entity API (8.4, DD-203, DD-204): the governance validation card the screen renders and the ValidateEntityClient that asks for it. The aurelius-atlas-validate-entity app imports its own response model from here.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client.models
items.text:
The governance-quality answer of the validate-entity API (CL-40, VE-02; DD-203).

The body the 8.3 mock answers — the four cards the webapp's editor renders, the AppSearchResult<GovQualitySearchObject> shape of the legacy libs/atlas/api::GovQualityApi (ADR 055 R4) — stated as models so a caller parses it and the app's constant is checked against one shape (VE-02, DV-67).

Every leaf is a {"raw": …} wrapper, and the doc-… ids, string compliant flags and _meta.engine of the mock are part of the browser contract, so they are modelled as they arrive, not normalised. The card keys and isNonCompliant are camelCase, the legacy's names.

Classes:

  • GovQualityItem –

    One governance check: a verdict item of a card.

  • GovQualityMeta –

    The _meta of an item: the engine, score and document id.

  • GovQualityValue –

    A {"raw": …} wrapper — every leaf of the governance document is one.

  • ValidationCard –

    One governance card: the items of one aspect, with the card's verdict.

  • ValidationResponse –

    The POST / answer: the four governance cards.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client.client
items.text:
The async client for the validate-entity API (CL-01..CL-05, CL-40; DD-203, DD-204, DD-205).

The shared client conventions of increment 8.4: constructed from an externally built httpx.AsyncClient and a token source, reading no environment variables (CL-01). The request path is relative, appended to that client's base URL, so a URL with a trailing slash — the str() of a pydantic HttpUrl — works as given (CL-01); the builder closes the pool, the API client never touches its lifecycle. Tests pass one built on a MockTransport and no socket opens (CL-02); the bearer goes on every call (CL-03); ValidateEntityClientError rises on a non-2xx answer (CL-04); httpx's own error propagates on an unreachable upstream (CL-05).

validate posts any mapping — the endpoint never reads the body (VE-01, DD-201), so the request is not a model — and parses the fixed governance document into a :class:~aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client.models.ValidationResponse (CL-40).

items.title: Styles
items.text: Design tokens shared by the Angular apps: aurelius-atlas-brand provides the Bulma-based theme the template's example frontend and aurelius-atlas-ui components are styled with.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-brand
items.text: This library provides the Aurelius brand styles and assets for use in Aurelius projects.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
You can include aurelius-atlas-brand styles in your project by adding them to your root styles.scss file:

@use "@aurelius/atlas-brand/src/main";

Then, you can include the aurelius-atlas-brand assets in your project by adding the following to your angular.json:

{
    "assets": [
        {
            "source": "libs/styles/aurelius-atlas-brand/assets",
            "target": "assets/aurelius-atlas-brand"
        }
    ]
}

Ensure the path points to the correct location of the aurelius-atlas-brand library.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas helps an organisation discover, understand, and trust its data — and stays easy to run, because a catalogue that is expensive to operate governs nothing. The engine behind that is a Python re-implementation of Apache Atlas 2.4.0 with Elasticsearch 9 as its only store. The two working records of the system are the conversion roadmap — the increments, their status and their semantics specs — and the architecture decisions, the ADRs that constrain every change. Both are kept current by every pull request.

What is a 'working record'?

A page that states the system's current truth and is updated by the pull requests that change it — unlike a reference page, which describes a planned state and is written once, by the increment that builds it. If a working record and the code disagree, the record is wrong.

The remaining trees are the reference architecture: they describe the system as it will stand when the plan is done. They are written increment by increment — each page names the increment that writes it, so a page is written in the pull request of that increment, while its facts are fresh (ADR 051). Pages not yet written carry a Planned marker naming their increment; the convention is in Documentation.

Why two kinds of pages

A mid-conversion system has no single accurate description: the code is the plan partly built. Splitting the records (what is true now, maintained by every PR) from the reference (what will be true, written as each increment lands) keeps both statements honest — each page names the increment, spec, or code that owns its facts.

items.title: The trees
items.text:
Tree Subject Written by Vision & Strategy Why the system exists, for whom, and where it is going written (ADRs 046–052, the roadmap) Data Lifecycle Management How catalogue data enters, lives, is shared, and is retired 0.2 → 6.3, per page Data Governance Types, lineage, quality, ownership, auditability 1.6 → 6.2, per page Platform Connectivity, delivery, observability, resilience, security 0.2 → 6.4, per page

Each tree index page carries its own per-page filling map.

These pages state the system's properties by role — the search store, the identity provider, the collector — so the description survives a change of product. The knobs, ports, and commands of each part live in its own documentation: the API Reference pages (design documentation per component), the Contributor Guide (cross-cutting how-tos), and each dev/ slice's README (development topology).

items.title: Self-hosted CI on AKS
items.text: Status: plan. Phase 0 (the hosted bridge) is merged; Phase 1 is next. Scope: moving the ci job of .github/workflows/ci.yaml from GitHub-hosted runners to self-hosted runners on AKS, run by Actions Runner Controller (ARC). The publish workflow (the dev container image itself) stays on hosted runners - it is the low-frequency builder of the thing the self-hosted runners consume.

items.title: Why
items.text:
The bridge (ADR 011 parity + devcontainers/ci) proved on hosted runners:

Evidence (2026-10-25) Result Full pipeline, one dev container, one job green 18m34s (validate 41s · test 4m14 · build+scan 66s · storybook 32s · sonar 9m41) Image mechanics 8.33 GB pull, warm ~101s, ~2m18s fixed setup per job DinD e2e compose + docker-build run on the dev container's own daemon Layer cache registry-backed (GHCR buildcache-*), survives the GitHub artifactcache outage that killed type=gha

What hosted still costs us: the 8.3 GB pull is paid per job (every runner is a fresh VM), the Actions cache is a 10 GB LRU pool behind Azure Front Door (its outage broke builds for hours), runner-minutes are billed, and queued PRs queue behind a pool we don't control. On AKS the image becomes a per-node containerd cache (paid once per node, not per run), caches become plain volumes, capacity is a node pool, and cost is nodes.

items.title: Target architecture
items.text:
flowchart LR
    GH[GitHub Actions<br/>workflow job] -->|job token| ARC[ARC controller<br/>gha-runner-scale-set-controller]
    ARC -->|creates per job| POD[runner pod<br/>ephemeral]
    subgraph NODE[AKS node pool: D8s v5, ephemeral OS disk]
        POD
        CD[containerd cache<br/>atlas-ci-runner:main<br/>pulled once per node]
        AF[Azure Files PVC<br/>.container-cache uv/npm/pre-commit]
    end
    POD -->|docker API tcp:2376| DIND[dind sidecar<br/>privileged]
    DIND -->|sibling containers| DC[dev container<br/>atlas-ci-runner:main]
    DC --> GHCR[(GHCR<br/>atlas-ci-runner:main<br/>buildcache-* tags)]
    CD -.pull.-> GHCR

The workflow, the composite action, and ci-pipeline.sh stay as they are - that is the point of the bridge. devcontainers/ci inside the runner pod talks to the ARC dind sidecar's daemon (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://localhost:2376) and starts the dev container as a sibling on it, exactly as on a hosted runner. Parity with the developer container is unchanged: same CLI, same lifecycle scripts, same image digest.

The one privileged dependency: the docker-in-docker feature marks the dev container privileged: true (it runs its own dockerd). A privileged sibling can only be created by a privileged daemon, so the ARC dind sidecar runs privileged. That is root-on-the-node by definition; it is contained by a dedicated node pool (taints + tolerations, no other workloads scheduled), a NetworkPolicy, and treating every pod on that pool as untrusted.

items.title: Shape: runner pod + dev container (recommended)
items.text:
Two shapes were considered; the first keeps the parity contract:

  • B - runner pod + devcontainers/ci (chosen): the runner pod is ARC's stock runner image; the pipeline runs in the dev container on the dind sidecar, i.e. the merged design moved machines. The dev==CI parity property (the reason for the bridge) survives untouched.
  • A - runner pod is atlas-ci-runner (later optimisation): set the runner container image to the dev container image and delete devcontainers/ci from the path - no sibling, no daemon exec. Cheaper per run, but the devcontainer lifecycle scripts (onCreateCommand/ postCreateCommand) stop running by construction and parity becomes "the image digest pins toolchain == dev" plus a bootstrap step. Only worth it once Phase 2 is boring.

items.title: What changes in the repo (Phase 1-2)
items.text:
Small by design - the bridge was built so this is a swap, not a rewrite:

Concern Hosted (today) AKS Change runs-on ubuntu-latest [self-hosted, linux, atlas-ci] repo config variable CI_RUNS_ON used in runs-on: - flip one variable to move the fleet, flip back to revert (flag day, per job) Disk cleanup step deletes preinstalled toolchains no-op (clean node) behind the existing disk-cleanup input; off on AKS actions/cache (features/toolchain caches) GitHub cache service (private repo + self-hosted = unavailable) volumes, below composite gates the two cache steps behind a use-actions-cache input; on AKS the same paths are a mounted volume and the steps are skipped uv/npm/pre-commit caches container-cache key, restore/save Azure Files PVC mounted at the same paths (.container-cache/) zero pipeline change - the UV_CACHE_DIR/npm_config_cache/PRE_COMMIT_HOME env already points there; volume = incremental, no 10 GB cap, no save step dev container image pulled per job pulled per node (containerd) imagePullSecrets (GHCR) on the pod template; node pool uses the ephemeral OS disk so containerd has room Docker layer cache registry (GHCR) registry - unchanged none (this is why the registry-cache switch pays off: it works from any machine) Artifacts, summaries, step outputs GitHub GitHub - self-hosted supported none Secrets (AGE_SECRET_KEY, Docker Hub, Chromatic) GitHub GitHub - ARC delivers job secrets to the runner pod none GHCR publish (buildcache-*) job token, packages: write same none

The publisher workflow, and every hosted-only workflow (scan, publish*, rotate-keys, the build check), stay hosted in Phases 1-2 - they are low-frequency and use the hosted cache service.

items.title: Infrastructure
items.text:
ARC with the Helm charts (gha-runner-scale-set-controller + gha-runner-scale-set), ephemeral per-job pods, GitHub App auth (not a PAT - App installs scope to the repo and survive rotation):

helm install arc \
    --namespace arc-systems --create-namespace \
    oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set-controller

helm install atlas-ci-runner \
    --namespace arc-runners --create-namespace \
    --set githubConfigUrl=https://github.com/aureliusenterprise/aurelius-atlas \
    --set githubConfigSecret=arc-atlas-runner-secrets \
    --set minRunners=0 --set maxRunners=3 \
    --set runnerScaleSetName=atlas-ci \
    --set template.spec.nodeSelector."kubernetes\.io/os"=linux \
    --set-string template.spec.tolerations[0].key=kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority \
    --set-string template.spec.tolerations[0].value=spot \
    -f arc-values.yaml \
    oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set

arc-values.yaml carries the three load-bearing blocks:

containerMode:
    type: dind
    dockerContainerTemplate:
        securityContext:
            privileged: true
        resources:
            requests: { cpu: 2, memory: 8Gi }
            limits: { cpu: 8, memory: 16Gi }
        volumeMounts:
            - name: dind-scratch
              mountPath: /var/lib/docker
template:
    spec:
        containers:
            - name: runner
              resources:
                  requests: { cpu: 4, memory: 16Gi }
                  limits: { cpu: 8, memory: 24Gi }
              volumeMounts:
                  - name: toolchain-cache
                    mountPath: /__w/aurelius-atlas/aurelius-atlas/.container-cache
        volumes:
            - name: dind-scratch
              emptyDir: {} # wiped per job; see node pool - NVMe temp disk below
            - name: toolchain-cache
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                  claimName: atlas-ci-toolchain-cache

Notes: the toolchain-cache PVC is Azure Files (NFS, ReadWriteMany) so the uv/npm/pre-commit caches are shared across nodes and persist across pods; /var/lib/docker on an emptyDir is wiped per job - nodes have ~610 GiB of NVMe temp disk (D8s v5), and with the AKS LocalPersistentVolume preview flag enabled, medium: LocalRaid moves the sidecar's overlay onto that NVMe; ARC's dind template wires DOCKER_HOST into the runner container. Node pool:

az aks nodepool add --resource-group <rg> --cluster-name <aks> \
    --name cipool --node-vm-size Standard_D8s_v5 \
    --node-count 1 --enable-auto-scaling --min-count 0 --max-count 3 \
    --kubelet-disk-type Ephemeral \
    --node-taints "ci=true:NoSchedule" --priority Spot --eviction-policy Delete

Standard_D8s_v5 (8 vCPU / 32 GiB / ~610 GiB NVMe temp): the pipeline peaks near 6 vCPU (test fan-out) and ~30 GB (ES + observability + buildkit). The pool is spot + minCount 0: it costs nothing between runs; a spot eviction mid-run is a failed job that requeues (jobs are idempotent; registry cache makes the rerun warm). GHCR pull secret:

kubectl -n arc-runners create secret docker-registry atlas-ghcr \
    --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<bot> --docker-password=<packages:read PAT>

...referenced as imagePullSecrets for the node's containerd pulls of atlas-ci-runner:main (and buildcache-* reads, which the in-container ghcr-login step already handles with the job token).

items.title: Phases
items.text:
Phase Scope Gate to pass Rollback 0 - bridge (done) whole pipeline in devcontainers/ci on hosted merged; green 18m34s revert workflow 1 - canary cluster, ARC, node pool, dind; validate-only job runs on [self-hosted, atlas-ci] beside hosted 5 consecutive green validate runs; GHCR pull cached on node (2nd run pull < 10s) delete scale set 2 - pipeline full ci job on AKS: volume-backed caches, CI_RUNS_ON flip; hosted kept warm via weekly cron run 10 green runs across PR types; wall clock ≤ hosted (18m34s); zero secret leaks in logs flip one variable 3 - steady state scale pool to demand; GHCR retention for buildcache-*; evaluate Shape A (runner = image) and moving the publisher 1 month, no infra tickets -

Phase 1's validate-only job is the same canary trick as the bridge: it exercises pull, dind, lifecycle scripts, caching, and the GHCR login path, in ~3 minutes, without spending test minutes on cluster bugs.

items.title: Risks and open questions
items.text:
• Privileged dind: accepted (dedicated spot pool, per-job wipe). If that ever stops being acceptable, the fallback is DooD: the runner pod mounts the node's containerd - which ARC does not support; the real fallback is Shape A, where the runner pod is the dev container and e2e moves to K8s-native test namespaces. Bigger lift, no privileged daemon.
  • Spot eviction = job requeue, not corruption; registry cache makes reruns cheap. If evictions get frequent, drop --priority Spot.
  • Azure Files latency for uv/npm caches over NFS: measure in Phase 2; the escape hatch is one PVC per node (no cross-node sharing, ReadWriteOnce)
    • the caches are content-addressed, so correctness survives.
  • ARC + actions/cache: not available for private repos on self-hosted - which is why the plan moves caches to volumes rather than proxying the cache API. Do not re-add a cache proxy casually.
  • Retention: buildcache-* tags need a GHCR cleanup policy (already a follow-up from the registry-cache switch) - AKS removes the hosted-only excuse.
  • Cost guard: maxRunners 3, pool max 3, spot, scale-to-zero. Steady-state estimate: an 18-minute run on D8s v5 spot ≈ $0.10, vs ~$0.32 hosted per run today - before counting the cache egress and queue waits the hosted pool adds.

items.title: Decisions to record
items.text: When Phase 1 starts, add an ADR (successor to the CI bridge decision): "CI runs on self-hosted ARC runners on AKS; the dev container remains the unit of execution; the publisher and low-frequency workflows stay hosted." Technical notes (ARC values, volume layout, CI_RUNS_ON flag day) belong in docs/architecture/conversion/design-log.md as DD-NNN entries.

items.title: Architecture Decisions
items.text: This section records architecture decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): short documents that capture a decision, the business situation that forced it, and the consequences it has. Code tells you what was built; an ADR tells you why — and the why is the part code cannot hand over.

items.title: The decision log
items.text:
New here? This is the whole set in one table. Read the records that govern the area you are about to work in; the rest can wait.

# Decision Status 001 Keep one monorepo for every stack — one repository, one entry point, atomic cross-stack change. Accepted 002 Modules are removable as whole slices — spine or optional capability, deleted in one pass. Accepted 003 Every project documents itself — knowledge beside what it describes, no central catalogue. Accepted 004 One shared domain model — one canonical definition per concept, generated or checked everywhere. Accepted 005 Development infrastructure starts with the app — one command to a running system. Accepted 006 The whole system runs on one machine — defects reproducible locally, validation without operated infrastructure. Accepted 007 One shared identity provider — one place people exist; surfaces only verify what it issues. Accepted 008 Real secrets encrypted, dev defaults committed — ciphertext travels with the code. Accepted 009 Every example runs and is tested — a broken example is removed, not annotated. Accepted 010 The unit validated is the unit that ships — one build per change, environments differ by settings only. Accepted 011 The development environment is a versioned artifact — one base for people and pipelines. Accepted 012 Validation runs against real services — a passing test is evidence about the shipped path. Accepted 013 Services prove who they are at every boundary — machine identity, separate from human identity. Accepted 014 The gate is defined once — the same rule set runs at commit time and in the pipeline. Accepted 015 A change answers for what it caused — change-caused findings block; world-state findings are reviewed on a cadence. Accepted 016 The system observes itself — traces, metrics, and logs never leave the boundary. Accepted 017 Shared concepts change only compatibly — additive by default, a breaking change becomes a new version. Accepted 018 Settings arrive at startup through one channel — read once, validated, failing loudly. Accepted 019 The system releases as one versioned whole — one number, one changelog, one release event. Accepted 020 Dependencies stay current by default — routine updates automatic, framework majors planned. Accepted 021 A new technology joins by recipe — discovered, gated, releasable, removable in one pass. Accepted 022 The codebase explains itself to its agents — nearest-first instructions for machine readers. Accepted 023 A storage schema changes only by recorded migration — one ordered path, data moved rather than replaced. Proposed 024 A validated release is promoted by a declared path — dev and test are the system's; beyond that, the deployment's. Accepted 025 Data has a stated lifetime — every kind expires on a named schedule the system enforces. Proposed 026 The system can be brought back from a named snapshot — backups stated, recovery rehearsed, loss bounded. Proposed 027 Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee — duplication and loss decided per stream, not defaulted. Proposed 028 Operational secret handling has a named owner — rotation, loss, and break-glass rehearsed, not invented. Accepted 029 What ships is signed and its origin provable — verification is part of delivery, not a later hope. Accepted 030 Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed — the agreement is stated once and drift fails the change. Accepted 031 Runtime versions have a declared support window — one answer per runtime, bumps planned, nothing floating. Accepted 032 Shared streams are named by a declared convention — the name says what flows and which version, never where. Accepted 033 Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory — what is in what we ran is a lookup, not a reconstruction. Accepted 034 Signals meet at one replaceable collection point — parts export to a seam, never to a backend directly. Accepted 035 Parts hand work through a durable event log — the log is the default integration; joining is a subscription. Accepted 036 The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary — the pipeline crosses at recorded points; the running system never does. Accepted 037 The system itself promises nothing about staying up — availability is what the deployment builds around it. Accepted 038 What a person may do is decided in one place — permission apart from identity; one answer, one act to revoke. Proposed 039 Data is protected where it travels and rests — declared arrangements, not assumed properties. Accepted 040 The system raises its hand when it is broken — named triggers, named destinations; silence is a condition. Proposed 041 A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path — response owned, written, practised. Accepted 042 Every dataset has an owner who answers for it — sharing is a stated answer, never an absence. Proposed 043 AI-assisted review informs the two signatures — it does not replace them, and its findings follow the blocking rule. Accepted 044 Every change carries two human signatures — the task owner who answers for it and a reviewer who confirms understanding. Accepted 045 Conventions are borrowed before they are invented — framework, then community, then invention; the preference outlives the brands. Accepted 046 The catalogue keeps its public contract while its implementation is replaced; every visible difference is a recorded deviation. Accepted 047 One search store is the only system of record for metadata — no separate graph, relational store or index. Accepted 048 Behaviour is proven against recorded responses of the reference implementation before it is accepted. Superseded by 052 049 Every function and every specified rule is traceable to a test, and the trace is published per change. Superseded by 056 050 The system carries only the capabilities the catalogue needs — a named deviation from the template spine. Accepted 051 The conversion proceeds in increments, each defined by a written specification before it is built. Accepted 052 Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source and its tests, each citing where; the reference is never run. Proposed 053 The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice, each slice specified before it is built. Proposed 054 The server API is the webapp's one data plane - the successor of the legacy app-search/Atlas split; other surfaces (identity, telemetry) stay allowed. Proposed 055 The lineage chain is a named data surface: the auxiliary APIs (lineage-model, data2model, validate-entity) join the server's surface set as a second family, superseding DD-140's lineage/validate exclusion. Proposed 056 Behaviour is proven by executed tests, not by a trace gate; the covers marker stays as a review convention. Accepted

items.title: Why record decisions
items.text:
• Decisions are inherited. Every codebase is read first by people who were not in the room — onboarding, handover, a fork. Without the reasoning, they cannot tell a deliberate constraint from an accident, and "fix" decisions that were the whole point.
  • Decisions outlive implementations. Frameworks and libraries change; the business reasoning behind a modular, removable design does not.
  • New contributors get the context. An ADR gives a reader the reasoning behind the wiring, so they can tell when a change would contradict an accepted decision.
  • Review has a reference. A pull request that quietly reverses an accepted decision is visible the moment it contradicts an ADR.

items.title: Keep decisions business-focused
items.text:
An ADR records a decision that constrains or enables business capabilities. Implementation detail — how a library is configured, which version of a framework is pinned — belongs in code and project documentation, not here.

The litmus test

Would this decision still matter if we replaced every technology in the stack? If yes, it is an ADR. If no, it is an implementation detail.

ADR material Not ADR material One shared domain model serves streaming and storage How pydantic-avro serialises a record Modules must be removable as whole slices Nx plugin configuration Real secrets are encrypted per project; only dev defaults are committed SOPS command-line flags Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it Docker Compose syntax Every project documents itself; no central catalogues Zensical navigation entries

Write the Context as a business situation (cost, risk, time-to-market, team autonomy, compliance), not as a technology comparison. Technologies may appear as evidence, but the drivers must stand without them.

State the Decision as a property that now holds, and name the current implementation only under Neutral / follow-ups. A record titled with a technology goes stale when the technology is replaced; a record titled with a property survives the replacement and says what replaced it.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
• Number records NNN-short-slug (e.g. 001-single-monorepo.md); numbers are never reused.
  • Statuses: Proposed → Accepted, then optionally Superseded (by a later record) or Deprecated.
Proposed or Accepted — what exactly is the test?

Where the mechanism lives, not how uniformly it is used. Accepted means the decision is made and the mechanism that makes it true exists in the spine of the system; a part that skips an existing mechanism is a named deviation in the record's follow-ups, which does not by itself block acceptance. Proposed means the decision is not yet made, or the mechanism does not yet exist where it must. A stated convention the parts follow is itself an enforcement point: the record is Accepted and a missing automated check is a named gap, not a Proposed status.

  • Never edit the decision of an accepted record. When the business situation changes, write a new record that supersedes it and update the old record's status line only.
  • When a record is superseded, check the records that cite it: a requirement borrowed from a superseded record no longer has a foundation, so the dependent record either adopts the requirement in its own words, cites the superseding record, or is itself revisited — recorded in a new record, not by editing the old decision.
  • Add each new record to the nav section of mkdocs.yaml.

items.title: Using ADRs
items.text:
• Start the log at 001 and keep the numbering consecutive; the log belongs to whoever maintains the codebase.
  • State every requirement in the record's own words. A requirement phrased as "the property NNN demands" outsources its foundation to another record: if that record is superseded, the requirement loses its reason for existing — the same failure the supersession rule above guards against, from the drafting side.
  • Reference the records that govern an area in pull requests touching it and link to them from the project documentation they explain.
