  • Each kept capability costs. Build time, dependency updates, security scanning, and reader attention — and it suggests to newcomers that it is part of the product.
  • The catalogue's needs are narrow. One HTTP service, one user interface, one data store (047), the shared identity provider, and observability.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 What is here is used. Every project in the repository serves the catalogue or its delivery workflow. R2 Template updates stay mergeable. The workflow parts of the template (pipeline, quality gate, documentation, secrets) stay recognisable so updates can be merged. R3 Nothing is removed before it is replaced. The repository builds and its tests pass after every removal.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Keep every template slice R1: unused code is maintained, scanned, and misread as product. Start from an empty repository, copy the workflow R2: template improvements can no longer be merged.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: What it buys
items.text: • A smaller, honest codebase; a faster pipeline; fewer dependency alerts.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: What it costs
items.text: • Re-adding event streaming later — for example, to accept Atlas hook notifications — means restoring the slice from the template.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Increment 0.1 removes the streaming and serverless slices and the Java build; increment 0.5 removes the example service, screen, library, and relational database when the Atlas server and dashboard replace them.
  • Until then, those examples remain a named deviation under this record.
The examples are harmless — why remove them?

Unused code is never harmless: it is built, scanned, updated, and defended in review, and a newcomer cannot tell an example from a feature (R1). Keeping them only until replacements exist is the disciplined version of the same rule — R3 sets the order, so the repository never loses a capability before it has its replacement.
path: 050. The system carries only what the catalogue needs

items.title: 051. The conversion proceeds in increments, each defined by a written specification
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-09
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The catalogue is converted in increments: one reviewable change, one named behaviour, one written specification that comes before the code. An increment is not complete until its rules are tested, its parity checks pass, and its decisions are recorded.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Increment, spec, code — in that order. The conversion proceeds in increments. Each is one change of reviewable size that ports one named behaviour, and it begins with a short written specification of that behaviour: scope, rules with identifiers, origin in the old system, deviations, and acceptance.

Definition of done. An increment is not complete until its rules are tested, its parity checks pass, and its decisions are recorded.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Context
items.text:
• A big-bang rewrite cannot be reviewed — and a review that cannot be done becomes a signature without understanding (044).
  • The old system is large and its behaviour is spread over many classes.
  • Without a stated scope per change, reviewers cannot tell an omission from a decision, and the project cannot tell how far it has come.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Reviewable size. A reviewer can understand one change in one sitting. R2 Stated meaning. What a change is supposed to do is written down before it is judged. R3 Measurable progress. At any moment it is clear which behaviours are done. R4 Decisions travel with the change. The reasons for a change are recorded in the same change, not reconstructed later.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Big-bang rewrite, reviewed at the end R1 and R3. Increments without written specs R1; R2: the code becomes its own specification, and review checks consistency, not intent. Feature tickets in an external tracker Partly meets R3; R4: the reasoning lives outside the repository and is lost with the tracker.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: What it buys
items.text: • Every change has a stated purpose and an objective definition of done; progress is visible in the repository itself.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Writing a specification takes time before any code exists.
  • Splitting large behaviours into increments occasionally needs temporary scaffolding.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The roadmap, specification template, and design log live in the conversion ledger; the pull request template asks for the increment and the records it touches.
Why specify before coding, when the spec may be wrong?

Because the spec is where a reviewer can object cheaply: written rules with identifiers can be argued with, tested, and cited (R2), while a merged implementation argues by existing. A spec that turns out wrong is amended in the open; an implementation that was silently wrong is found in production.
path: 051. The conversion proceeds in specified increments

items.title: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source, without running the reference
items.text:
• Status: Proposed (becomes Accepted when increment 0.4 provides the scenario harness)
  • Date: 2026-10-17
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Supersedes 048.

A ported behaviour is accepted only when it passes scenarios whose expectations are read from the reference implementation's source and its own tests, each scenario citing where it was read. The reference is never built, run, or recorded from.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Scenarios, cited. A ported behaviour is accepted only when it passes scenarios — requests with their expected responses — whose expectations are read from the source code and the own tests of the reference implementation, each scenario citing where it was read.

No running reference. No instance of the reference implementation is built, run, or recorded from.

Scenarios are code. They are stored with the code and reviewed like code; a comparison ignores only fields declared volatile, and a deliberate difference is declared with the deviation it belongs to.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Context
items.text:
The contract the new system must honour (046) is defined by a large existing implementation, not by a complete written specification. 048 proposed recording the responses of a running reference implementation.

  • The goal is independence. The conversion aims at a system that does not depend on the old one; operating the old system — even only to record from it — keeps a toolchain and an operational skill alive that the organisation wants to retire, and ties the work to building a large legacy codebase.
  • The source is enough. The reference's source code, its own tests, and its documentation remain available and fixed at one version.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Grounded expectations. Every expected response can be traced to a named place in the reference's source, tests, or documentation, so a reviewer can check it against something the implementers did not write. R2 Repeatable without the old system. No test run, and no step of writing a test, needs the reference implementation built or running. R3 Changes to expectations are visible. When what counts as correct changes, the change shows up in review. R4 Intended differences are explicit. A deliberate deviation is declared with its recorded deviation, and the comparison respects it rather than being silenced test by test.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Record from a running reference (048) The strongest oracle for R1; R2: someone must build and run the reference to record each new scenario. Hand-written expectations, uncited R1: the expectations encode the implementer's reading with nothing to check them against. Run the reference's own integration tests against the new system R1 for what they check; R2: their harness needs the reference's build — and they check too little of each response to protect the dashboard.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: What it buys
items.text: • No legacy toolchain in the loop; every expectation carries its evidence; everyday runs are fast and offline.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: What it costs
items.text: • Expectations encode our reading of the source, so behaviour that is hard to see in the code — serialisation details, ordering, error texts produced by frameworks — can be misread. Review must compare a scenario with its citation, and scenarios borrow the reference's own test fixtures verbatim where they exist.
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Current reference: the release-2.4.0 tag of Apache Atlas (DD-001).
  • The scenario format, runner, and comparison are test tooling; results appear in the published test report (049).
  • Shadowing production traffic of an existing Atlas remains possible later as a release check for a migrating customer.
If nobody runs the old system, how do you know your reading is right?

You don't know it from a machine — you know it from citations a reviewer can check: every expectation names the place in Atlas's source, tests, or docs it was read from (R1), and the reference's own test fixtures are borrowed verbatim where they exist. That is a weaker oracle than a running system, accepted deliberately: the running system's cost is the legacy toolchain the conversion exists to retire (R2).
path: 052. Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source

items.title: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-20
  • Deciders: Aurelius Atlas maintainers
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: Decision
items.text:
We will rewrite the Aurelius Atlas web interface in this workspace as apps/aurelius-atlas-webapp, one feature slice at a time, in current Angular idiom, and we will not port its custom patterns. The Aurelius web interface (apps/atlas in the aureliusenterprise/aurelius repository, Angular 17.3, 62 NgModules, a custom Redux wrapper, and 20 shared libraries) is the starting material. Its features survive; its architecture does not.

Three properties of the target are fixed, not per-slice choices:

  • State is signals. The custom store abstraction is removed outright and each slice's state becomes signal() and computed(). No adapter, no compatibility layer, no coexistence.
  • Presentational components are dumb and shared. A visual component with no service side effects lives in aurelius-atlas-ui, takes input() and emits output(), and ships a story. Application components keep their own state and are not shared.
  • Every slice is tested before it is accepted, by Vitest unit tests and by a Playwright end-to-end scenario. The Aurelius Jest suite is not carried over.

The Aurelius web interface keeps running untouched while this proceeds, and the template's example app stays as the pattern reference until the webapp replaces it (DD-019).
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: Context
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas re-implements the catalogue's server in Python (ADR 046). Its users, though, are served today by two interfaces that are both unsuitable as the destination:

  • The Apache Atlas dashboards are the reference implementation's UI — vendored and served at / and /n/ (DD-001). They are the parity yardstick, not a product Aurelius intends to maintain: Angular 8-era, Grunt-built, and explicitly frozen.
  • The Aurelius web interface is the product Aurelius does own and does want: five years of data-catalogue screens (search, browse, entity details, create and edit, governance quality, domains, lineage) built on the organisation's @models4insight platform.

That interface is expensive to keep. It sits four majors behind (17.3 against this workspace's 22.2), and its platform libraries carry patterns the workspace has since replaced — NgModule bootstrap, a hand-rolled Redux layer, a TranslateService abstraction, constructor injection, BehaviorSubject state. Upgrading it in place means crossing five ng update majors while those abstractions keep their old shape, and the result is Angular 22 running 2009 architecture.

The workspace also cannot host it as it stands: the target app bootstraps with bootstrapApplication and zoneless change detection, and @angular/platform-browser-dynamic — the package an NgModule bootstrap needs — is not installed at all. Serving the Aurelius interface from this workspace therefore requires the NgModule layer to go, not to be preserved.

The two forces in tension: the interface is the most valuable thing Aurelius has outside the server, and the fastest way to run it here is a mechanical upgrade that keeps all of it.
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• R1 — The interface runs in this workspace, on its Angular, its Nx, its CI, and its hardened image. It is not a second application with its own toolchain.
  • R2 — The Aurelius interface keeps running while this work proceeds. The port must not freeze the product that is serving users today.
  • R3 — No pattern is kept that the workspace has replaced. Signals for state, standalone components, the built-in localisation, Vitest and Playwright. A slice that ports a custom abstraction has not delivered its slice.
  • R4 — The work is reviewable in pieces a person can read (ADR 044). Each increment lands one coherent capability with its tests, not a bulk migration.
  • R5 — The Aurelius Jest suite is a source of behavioural knowledge, so the rules it asserts are re-expressed in the new tests rather than silently lost.
  • R6 — The Apache Atlas parity contract is untouched (ADR 048, ADR 052). The vendored dashboards stay as the reference UI for the REST contract.
  • R7 — Shared UI is shared once: a presentational component exists in aurelius-atlas-ui with a story, and styling comes from the brand tokens.
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
Upgrade in place, then modernise. Run the 17→22 ng update chain on the Aurelius app, vendor the result, and convert patterns afterwards. Cheapest route to a running Angular 22 app, and it satisfies R1 and R2. It fails R3 by construction — the app ships with its NgModule graph, Redux store, and TranslateService intact, and R4 turns the modernisation into one migration PR of tens of thousands of lines. It also needs the deprecated platform-browser-dynamic package installed, i.e. the workspace must add a dependency it has decided not to use. Rejected.

Serve the Aurelius app unchanged from the Python server, as an external artifact. Satisfies R1's deployment and touches nothing. It fails R3 entirely and leaves Aurelius with two Angular toolchains, two dependency trees, and two security postures to maintain — the opposite of adopting this workspace. Rejected.

Port into aurelius-atlas-frontend-example, the app that already demonstrates the target conventions. Removes the need for a new project and keeps one Angular app in the workspace. It fails R4: the example is deliberately small and legible as a pattern reference, and merging ~1,000 files of migrated product code into it destroys the thing it is for. Rejected.

Rewrite the interface from scratch, keeping only the REST client. Cleanest architecture and the best chance at R3. It fails R2 and R5 — five years of screen behaviour and the knowledge in 50 Jest suites are discarded, and nothing ships until the whole rewrite lands. Rejected.

Rewrite slice by slice in a new project, keeping the Aurelius app running — the decision. Satisfies R1 through R7. Its cost is duplication during the transition and a source tree with two copies of the same product, paid for legibility and reversibility.
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: Aurelius gains a web interface on this workspace's dependency set, built the way the rest of the system is built. Signals replace the custom store, which removes a layer readers of the code must learn before they can follow any screen. Each slice is a reviewable PR with its own tests, and the Aurelius app keeps serving, so the work is reversible at every boundary.
  • Negative: the same screens exist in two codebases until the last slice lands, and Aurelius keeps paying for a four-major-behind Angular while the port proceeds. Behaviour is re-expressed, not inherited, so a rule asserted only in a Jest test and missed in review is a real regression risk (R5 is the mitigation, and it is manual). There is no compatibility layer to fall back on: a slice that lands with Redux in it is a defect, not a state.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: the Aurelius interface becomes the served UI at some point in this track, which supersedes the plan to serve the Atlas dashboards at / (DV-64). The example app and the template's Angular toolchain then leave with it (DD-019). The track is scheduled as increments 7.x in the conversion ledger and starts with the application shell (7.1), the one slice with no dependency on the catalogue API.
path: 053. The webapp is rewritten in Angular idiom, slice by slice

items.title: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane: the consolidated Aurelius Atlas server
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One server, one data plane, one client. Every data call the webapp makes — catalogue, search, and every catalogue surface that follows — goes to the Aurelius Atlas server's API, composed from the single runtime-configured base URL (apiBaseUrl, today /api). The webapp names no second data host, port, prefix, or search engine, and no second data-plane token.

The scope is the data plane, not every socket. The server is the successor of the legacy split — the surface that replaces App Search and the Apache Atlas APIs — and that is the whole of what this decision fixes. It is not a ban on other surfaces: the webapp already reaches Keycloak (sign-in, token refresh, the silent-SSO iframe) and the OpenTelemetry collector, and a future slice may add another. Those are not data planes; each is named at the deployment boundary (the CSP) and recorded by the increment that adds it. A new data surface is the event this decision governs, and needs its own record.

The legacy split is retired, not ported. The Aurelius application split metadata across two systems: the Apache Atlas catalogue (its REST API) and a third-party search backend carrying the search, governance-quality, and data-quality surfaces (the /elastic, /gov_quality, /data_quality endpoints). Aurelius Atlas consolidates both into the server: search is an endpoint family of the catalogue API (increment 4.1, built on the one store of 047), and the third-party search surface has no Aurelius Atlas backend and is not ported — its client methods exist only for endpoints the server answers (DD-140).

Today this is a stated rule over verified fact, not new work: the ported client library (7.3) injects one API_BASE_URL and composes every data URL from it (APC-01), the webapp contains no App Search remnants, and the served webapp's content-security policy keeps connect-src 'self' for the data plane, widened only for Keycloak's origins (APC-05) — the exception list is the deployment's, and the e2e CSP scenario proves the baseline.
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: Context
items.text: The legacy application's split was a fact of its history: Atlas held the catalogue, the search backend held the searchable copies plus the governance features, and keeping them in step was the product's burden. Aurelius Atlas replaces the split with one store (047) and keeps Atlas's public contract (046). The webapp port (7.x) inherits the legacy's two-client shape and must state, once, which API the new product speaks — before the search slice (7.4) decides by omission.
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• R1 — One data endpoint surface. Every data call the webapp makes goes to the server; the runtime configuration carries one API base URL. Non-data surfaces (identity, telemetry) are the webapp's to reach, named at the deployment boundary.
  • R2 — The public contract stays Atlas's (046): the server's endpoints are the Atlas paths, and the parity harness keeps reading the Atlas reference for them.
  • R3 — Search is the server's (047): no second index, no third-party engine, in the webapp's view of the system.
  • R4 — The client stays honest (DD-140): client methods exist only for endpoints the server answers, so specs and e2e never assert a backend that will not exist.
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Keep the legacy split. Port the search-backend client as Aurelius shipped it: a second system of record with no Aurelius Atlas backend — the wire format of a dependency this product rejects (047, 050). Fails R3, R4.
  • Proxy the split behind the server. The server forwards search to a third-party engine: one URL, two systems of record, and a dependency the deployment must run. Fails R3; pays R1's letter to break its purpose.
  • Consolidate later. Port the split, fold search in when 4.1 lands: dead clients at day one (DD-140's audit finding verbatim) and an origin/auth story left open through the 7.x track. Fails R1 for the whole interim.
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: one data origin (CSP connect-src 'self' holds for /api, proven in e2e), one bearer token on every data call (APC-06, 6.1), one wire format to keep parity with; the search slice is a thin client over an endpoint family, not a second stack.
  • Negative: search is blocked on the server's 4.1 — the hold DD-140 and DD-143 already accepted; 7.4's client is specified from the Atlas source (052) as 4.1's spec lands, not guessed from the legacy's search-backend DTOs. A future data surface is an ADR event, not a pull request — the friction is the point, and the price of it.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: the non-data surfaces today are Keycloak (cross-origin, whitelisted in the CSP — APC-05) and the OTel collector (same-origin /otel proxy, SHL-11); a future slice may add more, and this record does not stand in their way. The workspace's EntitiesService in aurelius-atlas-data-access is the FastAPI example's CRUD/SSE client — a template example, not a second data plane; it retires with the examples at 7.10 (DV-64, DD-019).
path: 054. The server API is the webapp's one data plane

items.title: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface: the auxiliary APIs join the server's surface set
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-11-08
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
  • Supersedes: the lineage and validate rows of DD-140
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The Aurelius lineage chain is a data surface of Aurelius Atlas, named here. The legacy application renders its lineage graph from two small backend services — lineage_model (flattens a dataset's upstream/downstream m4i_*_process relations into archimate rows) and data2model (turns those rows into an ar3 model string the diagram library draws) — and a validation mock, validate_entity. Aurelius Atlas ports all three as FastAPI services: apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model, apps/aurelius-atlas-data2model, and apps/aurelius-atlas-validate-entity (increments 8.1–8.3).

This is the ADR event 054 requires for a new data surface: the auxiliary APIs are the second data surface family of the product, each app deployed at its own origin, named at the deployment boundary (the CSP, increment 8.4) when the webapp starts calling them.

What 054 keeps. One token (the Keycloak bearer), one auth library (aurelius-atlas-auth, increment 8.0), Atlas's wire-contract discipline — extended to Aurelius-origin endpoints by citing the Aurelius source as the reference (052's rule, applied to a non-Atlas reference: the legacy services in .scratch/aurelius). The consolidation rule stands for everything it named: search stays the server's (047), the App Search surface stays unported, and the legacy catalogue APIs (entity, glossary, relationship) stay the server's Atlas paths (046).

What 054 relaxes, and only here. DD-140 excluded the lineage and validate clients because "the lineage/validate/dashboard backends are separate services with no Aurelius equivalent" — the exclusion was about a backend that would never exist. This increment builds the backend, so the exclusion retires for lineage and validate. It stands unchanged for the App Search trio (/elastic, /gov_quality, /data_quality) and the dashboard backend: those have no Aurelius Atlas system of record and are not ported.

The data path is stubbed at first, the API ships real. 8.1–8.3 read the lineage feed from a configurable Atlas base URL (GET /v2/lineage/{guid}) with fixtures; the server's real lineage work is increment 5.1, and the lineage-model app's wiring to it is 5.1's delivery. Shipping the API first keeps each increment one slice (051).
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: Context
items.text: The webapp track (7.x) ports the screens; the lineage graph is the one screen family whose backend does not exist in this workspace. The legacy chain is small (three services, a few hundred lines each), its contracts are fully readable in source, and the ar3 JSON the diagram library consumes is specified by the legacy parsers — a portable surface with no third-party dependency once m4i-analytics is reimplemented natively (DV-68). Leaving it unported would leave the webapp's lineage slices (7.x) permanently unwired.
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• R1 — One identity story. All three apps verify the same Keycloak tokens through aurelius-atlas-auth (8.0's rules AUX-04/05); no app invents an auth path.
  • R2 — One deployment shape. FastAPI apps with the workspace's Docker, healthcheck, env-prefix, SOPS, and OTel conventions; per-service otel-<service> ingest identities (DD-197).
  • R3 — The browser contract is the legacy contract. The JSON shapes the legacy services return ({model, metadata} for data2model, the flattened rows for lineage-model) are kept verbatim; the ar3 string is consumed by the webapp's existing archimate3 parser (7.x) without changes.
  • R4 — Parity cites Aurelius source. Every rule of 8.1–8.3 names the legacy file it ports; there is no Atlas 2.4 counterpart (these endpoints exist in no Apache product), and no live Java/Aurelius system is run.
  • R5 — The data path lands with 5.1. 8.x fixtures stand in for the real feed; the apps keep one configurable upstream and no hardcoded host.
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Fold the chain into the server. One app, three route groups: fewer containers, but the server's ADR 046 parity surface gains non-Atlas paths, its image gains the layout engine, and 051's increment sizes break. Refused.
  • Keep m4i-analytics. Port the legacy ar3 library (pandas, graphviz, bokeh, ~2k lines) as a workspace lib: a dependency of a retired product for a JSON string the webapp only needs to be ar3-shaped. Native reimplementation (DV-68) keeps the browser contract and drops the tree. Refused.
  • Server-side lineage feed first (5.1 before 8.x). The real data path before the APIs: 5.1 grows lineage semantics without a consumer to specify them, and 8.x stays blocked. Refused — stub first (this ADR's data-path rule).
  • One app for all three services. One container, /lineage_model, /data2model, /validate_entity route groups: fewer images, but each legacy service has its own scaling, health, and env story, and the user's deployment decision names one app per legacy service. Refused.
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The webapp gains a lineage screen family with a working backend path (8.4+): its CSP widens to the auxiliary origins, named at deployment.
  • The deployment topology grows three stateless containers (plus their OTel/Keycloak plumbing, 8.0) — all stateless, no new store; the lineage data stays in the server's store (047), read through /v2/lineage/{guid}.
  • deviations.md records the deliberate divergences: DV-67 (validate-entity ships as the legacy mock), DV-68 (native ar3 layout replaces m4i-analytics), DV-69 (lineage source stubbed until 5.1).
  • DD-140's audit note stays as history; its lineage/validate exclusion is superseded by this record, its App Search exclusion stands.
path: 055. The lineage chain is a named data surface

items.title: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests, not by a trace gate
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-24
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise
  • Supersedes: 049

The pipeline proves a change by running its tests — unit, parity scenarios, end-to-end — and nothing else. It no longer gates a merge on a traceability check, and it publishes no per-change trace report. Naming what a test covers stays a code-review convention: the covers marker and the trace tool remain, as a local aid.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Executed behaviour is the gate. A change merges when its tests pass; the pipeline refuses a change that fails a test, not a change whose coverage markers have gaps. The desired behaviour of the catalogue is encoded in the unit, parity, and end-to-end suites, and those executed results — with the coverage gate (ADR 015) — are the evidence a reviewer signs against.

The trace stays as a convention, not a gate. Tests keep naming what they prove via @pytest.mark.covers; reviewers use the names to find the test behind a rule. aurelius-atlas-trace check and report remain local tools, run by whoever wants their answer. The pipeline runs neither.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: Context
items.text: ADR 049 (increment 0.3) required every public function and every specified rule id to be named by a collected marker, with the pipeline refusing gaps and publishing one trace report per change. In practice the requirement duplicated what the suites already prove: the desired behaviour of each increment is encoded in its unit tests, which run on every change, while the check proves only that a test names a target — a declaration, collection-only, never an executed result. Keeping the declaration true across the whole surface (TypeScript citations, end-to-end claims, cross-project rules) consumed pipeline stages and review attention without adding evidence, and its gaps surfaced as CI noise rather than as missing tests.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Executed proof. What blocks a merge is the result of running tests, not files. R2 No duplicated proof. One place states what a test is for; bookkeeping on top is noise. R3 Reviewable evidence. A reviewer sees, in the change, the tests and results behind it. R4 Cheap convention. Naming what a test proves stays available and does not block.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Keep the gate as specified (049) R1: the check proves naming, not behaviour; R2: it restates what the unit tests already encode. Widen the gate (citations for TypeScript, e2e) R2: more mechanism proving the same declarations, more pipeline and review cost, still no executed result. Manual traceability matrix 049's own objection: the document drifts from the code on the first busy week. Drop the marker convention as well R3: reviewers lose the pointer from a rule id to the test that proves it.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: Tradeoffs
items.text:
• Positive: the pipeline is smaller and says only what it can prove — a failed test; no marker bookkeeping blocks a merge; the suites stay the single source of intended behaviour.
  • Negative: an untested function is no longer surfaced as a pipeline gap; coverage percentage (the SonarQube gate) and review are what catch it. The per-change published trace report is gone.
  • Neutral / follow-ups: parity scenarios keep their citation discipline (ADR 052) — that is how expected behaviour is justified, and it is unchanged. The trace lib stays for local use and is removable as a slice when the convention fades.
path: 056. Behaviour is proven by executed tests

items.title: ADR Template
items.text:
Copy the template below into docs/architecture/adr/NNN-short-slug.md (next free number, kebab-case slug), fill it in, and add the new file to the nav section of mkdocs.yaml. Delete the guidance comments when you are done.

Keep the record business-focused: describe the decision's drivers and consequences, not implementation detail. If replacing every technology in the stack would make the record wrong, it needs rewriting. See Architecture Decisions for the full practice.

# NNN. Decision Title

<!--
    Title the decision as an action or a property that now holds, not a topic:
    "Adopt a single shared domain model", not "Domain model".
-->

- **Status:** Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by [NNN](./NNN-slug.md) |
  Deprecated
- **Date:** YYYY-MM-DD (date of last status change)
- **Deciders:** names or roles who own this decision

## Decision

<!--
    The decision itself, in one or two sentences, active voice: "We will ...".
    State what is now true and what the organisation may and may not do
    because of it.
    If the decision has sharp edges, name them here rather than hiding them.
    The decision comes first on purpose: the sections below justify it, they
    do not build up to it. Draft them first, though — a decision written
    before the requirements is a solution looking for a problem.
-->

## Context

<!--
    The business situation that makes a decision necessary: the goal, the
    constraints, and the forces in tension (cost, risk, delivery speed, team
    autonomy, compliance, portability). Describe the problem as it would be
    described to a non-technical stakeholder, and keep it neutral: do not
    argue for the decision here, and do not phrase the situation in terms
    only the chosen option could solve. Technologies may appear as evidence,
    but the drivers must stand without them.
-->

## Requirements

<!--
    What any acceptable solution must deliver, independent of the chosen one:
    short "must" statements (R1, R2, ...) that a reader can grade the
    alternatives against. Every rejected alternative should fail at least one
    requirement; the decision should satisfy all of them.
-->

## Alternatives

<!--
    The realistic alternatives to the decision (including "do nothing"), each
    described fairly and graded against the requirements, with the reason it
    lost. One short paragraph per option. This section is the main thing
    future readers mine — they need to know the alternatives were weighed,
    not that the chosen option was perfect.
-->

## Tradeoffs

<!--
    What follows from the decision — both directions, honestly. If a
    consequence is "this must be revisited when X", say so explicitly.
-->

- **Positive:** capabilities, guarantees, or costs avoided.
- **Negative:** new costs, constraints, or risks accepted.
- **Neutral / follow-ups:** things this decision makes necessary but does not
  itself deliver.

Reference related records inline, where they are relevant, rather than in a
trailing links section.

items.title: Conversion
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas re-implements Apache Atlas 2.4.0 in Python with Elasticsearch 9 as its only store, keeping the REST API and the dashboard (ADR 046, ADR 047). The work proceeds in increments (ADR 051); this page is the roadmap and the status of each one.

The ledger in this section is the central record of the conversion:

Page What it holds Design Log Numbered technical decisions (DD-NNN), never edited once accepted Java to Python Map Which Java module or class becomes which Python module, and its status Deviations from Apache Atlas Every intended behaviour difference, referenced by the parity report Increments The semantics specification of each increment

items.title: Definition of done for an increment
items.text:
graph LR
    S[Semantics spec] -->|PR| C[Code + scenarios]
    C -->|parity + trace green| R[Two approvals]
    R -->|merged| D[Done]
    D -.->|records| L[Design log, Java map, deviations]

An increment is specified before it is built and proven before it is accepted (ADR 051). The checks a PR must pass:

  • Semantics spec in increments/, every rule has an id
  • Every new public function has a test that names it (@pytest.mark.covers)
  • Every rule id is named by at least one test
  • Parity scenarios for the endpoints in scope pass, each citing its Atlas source (ADR 052)
  • nx affected -t lint typecheck test e2e -c ci is green and the coverage gate holds
  • Design log, Java map and deviations updated; ADR written if a business-level decision was made
  • Conventional-commit title and two human approvals

items.title: After phase 0
items.text:
Two expat CVEs and a musl CVE are accepted on a temporary basis

CVE-2026-77214 and CVE-2026-102633 (expat/libexpat 2.8.5-r1, from the server image's hardened base) are fixed upstream in 2.9.0-r0 but accepted in SonarCloud because no hardened base image carried the fix yet; so is CVE-2026-107891 (musl 1.2.6-r2, from the frontend example image's hardened base, fixed in 1.2.6-r3). The acceptance expires with the next base-image refresh — the checklist below is the re-decision, and an accepted risk that nobody re-checks is drift.

To do once the last 0.x increment is done:

  • Re-check the accepted expat vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-77214 and CVE-2026-102633 in expat and libexpat 2.8.5-r1 come from the base image dhi.io/python:3.14-alpine3.24 of aurelius-atlas-server, and are fixed in 2.9.0-r0. They were accepted in SonarCloud on #85, because no hardened image with the fix existed yet. Before closing them:
    • Check that the current base image ships expat 2.9.0 or later.
    • Check that SonarCloud has closed the four issues as fixed.
    • If either check fails, reopen the issues and decide again.
  • Re-check the accepted musl vulnerability. CVE-2026-107891 in musl and musl-utils 1.2.6-r2 comes from the base image dhi.io/nginx:1.30-alpine3.24 of aurelius-atlas-frontend-example, and is fixed in 1.2.6-r3. It was accepted in SonarCloud on #139, because no hardened image with the fix existed yet. Before closing it:
    • Check that the current base image ships musl 1.2.6-r3 or later.
    • Check that SonarCloud has closed the two issues as fixed.
    • If either check fails, reopen the issues and decide again.

items.title: After the plan
items.text:
To do once 6.4 is done, not numbered as an increment yet (DD-019):

  • Remove the template's examples. The FastAPI example service, the Angular example screen, aurelius-atlas-example, aurelius-atlas-sdk, libs/angular/*, libs/styles, dev/postgres and the Angular, Storybook and Chromatic toolchain leave (ADR 050).
    • dev/keycloak stays for 6.1 and takes over pg_hba.conf from dev/postgres.
    • The rules are tested by a test-only tools/workspace project without a Sonar target.
    • They are kept until then because the project's second phase needs them again.

items.title: Design Log
items.text: Technical decisions made during the conversion that are too implementation-specific for an ADR but must not be lost: storage layout, identifiers, query translation, test tooling. Business-level decisions are ADRs in Architecture Decisions.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Entries are numbered DD-NNN, consecutively; numbers are never reused.
  • Statuses: Proposed → Accepted, then optionally Superseded by DD-NNN.
  • An accepted entry is never edited except its status line. A changed decision is a new entry that supersedes the old one.
  • Every entry names the increment that introduced it, so the reasoning can be found next to the code and the specification it belongs to.
  • An increment that makes a decision adds its entry in the same pull request.

items.title: Entry template
items.text:
### DD-NNN. Decision as a statement

- **Status:** Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by DD-NNN
- **Increment:** N.N
- **Date:** YYYY-MM-DD

**Decision.** What we do, in one or two sentences.

**Reason.** Why, in terms of the requirements of the increment.

**Alternatives.** What else was considered and why it lost.

**Consequences.** What follows, including what must be revisited and when.

items.title: DD-001. Reference is Apache Atlas 2.4.0, and both dashboards are served
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Increment: 0.1
  • Date: 2026-10-09

Decision. The behaviour to reproduce is that of the release-2.4.0 tag of Apache Atlas. Both of its user interfaces are served unchanged at the paths Atlas uses: dashboardv2 at / and dashboardv3 at /n/. End-to-end tests cover dashboardv3 in depth and dashboardv2 with a smoke test.

Reason. Parity tests need one fixed reference (ADR 048), and 2.4.0 is the latest Apache Atlas release. Atlas 2.4.0 serves the classic interface at the root and the newer one under /n/, and each links to the other; serving both keeps every bookmark and link working at the cost of one more static build, whereas dropping one would be a visible deviation.

Alternatives. Track Atlas master: unstable fixtures, no released artefact to compare against. Serve only dashboardv3 and redirect / to /n/: one build less, but breaks the switch-back link and existing bookmarks, and would need a deviation entry.

Consequences. A move to a later Atlas release is a new entry plus a re-recording of all fixtures. Features used only by dashboardv2 still need backend support; they are found by its smoke test.

items.title: DD-002. Atlas code lives in aurelius-atlas projects split by layer
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Increment: 0.1
  • Date: 2026-10-09

Decision. Atlas code is split into workspace projects by layer, all prefixed aurelius-atlas- (Python packages aurelius_atlas_*): -model (data shapes, no I/O), -typesystem (type registry and validation), -store-es (Elasticsearch access), -core (stores and services), -dsl (query language), apps/aurelius-atlas-server (REST), apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard (UI), reports/aurelius-atlas-test-report, plus dev/elasticsearch and dev/atlas-reference.

Reason. Layers that do not do I/O can be unit-tested without infrastructure; the dependency direction (model ← typesystem ← core → store-es; server → core) keeps each increment's change local, and each project follows an existing template recipe. The aurelius prefix keeps the organisation's naming convention.

Alternatives. One large package mirroring the Java module tree: simpler imports, but every change touches the same project and nothing can be tested in isolation. A package per Java module (intg, repository, webapp): mirrors history rather than the dependency structure we want.

Consequences. Projects are created by the increment that first needs them, not up front.

items.title: DD-003. Template projects are renamed to the aurelius-atlas prefix
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Increment: 0.1
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. All workspace projects inherited from the template carry the aurelius-atlas- prefix (directories, Nx names, uv/npm package names, Python import packages, env-var prefixes, Sonar keys, compose project and network names, Grafana dashboards). The org handle aureliusenterprise, the npm scope @aurelius, the Keycloak client/realm ids (aurelius, master), and the DB name (aurelius) are identities of the organisation/Keycloak and stay unchanged.

Reason. DD-002 fixes the aurelius-atlas- prefix for the Atlas projects; renaming the template examples now, while they are the only content, avoids two naming generations in one repo and the churn of renaming them piecemeal once Atlas code lands beside them.

Alternatives. Rename only new Atlas projects: leaves aurelius-* and aurelius-atlas-* side by side, which reads as two projects with different ownership. Keep the template names entirely: makes the eventual atlas-vs-template distinction implicit rather than visible in the project graph.

Consequences. Docker image names change (ghcr.io/aureliusenterprise/aurelius-atlas-*); Sonar projects, Chromatic, and any external CI references must be created/renamed to match. .env.enc files were re-encrypted with the new prefixed keys. Old locally built images are stale and should be pruned (docker image prune / rebuild via nx e2e).

items.title: DD-004. The SPA keeps tokens in memory and renews them silently
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Increment: 0.1
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The Angular SPA uses Keycloak's default in-memory token store (tokenStore: "default" in provideKeycloak, apps/aurelius-atlas-frontend-example/src/app/app.config.ts) with onLoad: "check-sso" and a silent-SSO redirect (/silent-check-sso.html). Access and refresh tokens never touch localStorage or any other persistent browser storage.

Reason. localStorage is readable by any script that achieves XSS on the origin, and is also exposed to browser extensions with host permissions; a stolen refresh token there is a durable session hijack. With the in-memory store, injected script can read the current access token but the attacker's code dies with the page, and a reload forces a fresh authentication check against Keycloak rather than replaying stored secrets.

Alternatives. tokenStore: "sessionStorage": survives reload in the tab, but every XSS or extension read is still one getItem away — same theft surface, no meaningful gain. tokenStore: "localStorage": survives tab close; strongest theft value, rejected. A confidential client with a BFF holding tokens server-side: the right answer at scale, deferred as its own increment — it changes the auth topology (new service, cookie session) rather than a setting.

Consequences. A page reload re-mints tokens via silent SSO; the user sees no login unless the Keycloak SSO session itself has ended. Silent SSO relies on a third-party-cookie-acceptable (or same-site) Keycloak deployment: where browsers block the framing cookie, check-sso degrades to a not-signed-in state and the app falls back to a full redirect login (login()), which still works. If per-tab token durability becomes a product requirement, supersede this entry by adding the BFF — not by moving the tokens to storage.

items.title: DD-005. The store uses the official async Elasticsearch client
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. aurelius-atlas-store-es talks to Elasticsearch through AsyncElasticsearch from the official elasticsearch Python client, version 9.5 or later within major 9, matching the 9.5 server (dhi.io/elasticsearch:9.5-debian13; minor upgrades are deliberate, patch releases follow the tag). A store instance owns exactly one client, opened and closed with the store (async with).

Reason. The server is FastAPI and asynchronous; a blocking client would tie up the event loop or need a thread pool. The official client tracks the server's API and versioning, ships typed request helpers, and includes the query DSL module that search (4.x) will need.

Alternatives. httpx against the REST API directly: no extra dependency, but every API, retry and error type would be rebuilt by hand. opensearch-py: a different server; ADR 047 names Elasticsearch. One client per request: simple, but loses connection pooling.

Consequences. The client's major version moves with the server's (STO-04 guards it). Connection pooling and retries are the client's; tuning them is part of 6.4.

items.title: DD-006. Development and tests run Elasticsearch with security on
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. dev/elasticsearch and the test fixture run with xpack.security enabled: TLS on the HTTP layer with a certificate from the workspace CA (dev) or an ephemeral CA (tests), and basic authentication for the built-in elastic user. The store library has no option to skip certificate verification.

Reason. It is the posture production needs, and the one dev/postgres already has; a store that only ever ran without security would meet TLS and authentication for the first time in production.

Alternatives. Security disabled in development: faster start-up and simpler curl, but a different code path (plain HTTP, no credentials) from production, and a verification switch in the library that someone eventually leaves off.

Consequences. Dev tools need the CA file and the password (curl --cacert dev/elasticsearch/certs/ca.pem -u elastic:…). A dedicated application user with least privilege replaces elastic when authorization arrives (6.2).

items.title: DD-007. The Elasticsearch test fixture ships with the store library
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The testcontainers helper that starts a TLS-enabled Elasticsearch lives in aurelius_atlas_store_es.testing, behind the library's testing extra, next to the code it serves.

Reason. Every later project with a store (-core, the server, the parity harness) needs the same container; the library that defines the settings is the one that knows how to build them for a test server, and keeping both together means a settings change cannot break the fixture unnoticed.

Alternatives. aurelius-atlas-sdk.testing, where the Postgres helper lives: would make the generic SDK depend on Elasticsearch. A copy per project: drifts.

Consequences. Test-only dependencies (testcontainers, trustme) stay out of the runtime install; consuming projects add aurelius-atlas-store-es[testing] to their dev dependencies.

items.title: DD-008. A yellow cluster is healthy
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The store's health check reports up for cluster status green or yellow and down for red (STO-05).

Reason. Yellow means every primary shard is assigned and all data is readable and writable; only replicas are missing. A single-node cluster, the development and small-installation case (ADR 006), is yellow as soon as an index has a replica. Reporting it down would make every single-node deployment permanently unready.

Alternatives. Green only: correct for multi-node clusters, unusable for single-node ones unless every index is created with zero replicas. A configurable threshold: one more setting nobody sets.

Consequences. Lost redundancy is not visible as a health failure; it is visible in the cluster metrics (ESD-06) and should be alerted on there.

items.title: DD-009. Traceability is checked from collected markers, not from a test run
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.3
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. aurelius-atlas-trace check runs pytest --collect-only over the unit and end-to-end tests of every Atlas project and reads the covers markers from the collected items. Whether the naming tests pass is the test job's concern, not the check's.

Reason. CI runs nx affected -t test e2e, so the results of one run contain only the affected projects' tests; a check over them would report every unaffected function as uncovered (TRC-10). Collection imports the tests but starts no containers, so it is cheap enough to run on every change.

Alternatives. Merge the trace files of the run with those of the last run on main: needs artifact plumbing between workflows and still goes stale when a run on main fails. Run every test on every change: correct, but turns a one-minute check into the full end-to-end suite. Parse the test sources with ast: misses markers applied through pytestmark, classes and parametrisation.

Consequences. A test module that fails to import fails the check, which is the right answer: its markers are unknown. A test that names a function but is skipped still counts as naming it; the report shows it as skipped.

items.title: DD-010. The traceability check covers Atlas code from increment 0.2 on
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.3
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. R1 applies to the public functions, methods and properties of every uv workspace member that the configuration does not exclude; the template projects (examples, SDK, reports) are excluded, and so are testing subpackages, which are test infrastructure. R2 applies to the rules of every specification from increment 0.2 on. The configuration is the [tool.aurelius-atlas-trace] table of the root pyproject.toml.

Reason. Template code is removed or replaced by the conversion (0.5 removes the examples), so markers on it would be written to be deleted. Excluding instead of listing makes a new Atlas project checked by default. Increment 0.1's rules (ADO-01 to ADO-03) describe the adoption of the template and were verified when it merged; 0.2 is the first increment with code, and its manual checks of ESD-01 to ESD-06 are replaced by tests in this increment.

Alternatives. Check every workspace member: retrofits markers onto code about to be deleted. List the Atlas projects explicitly: a new project is silently unchecked until someone adds it.

Consequences. A project that leaves the template set (the SDK, if it is kept) is removed from the exclusion list and gets its markers in the same change.

items.title: DD-011. The test report is generated from JUnit, coverage and trace files
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.3
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. aurelius-atlas-trace report turns JUnit XML (pytest --junitxml), Cobertura XML (pytest-cov) and the plugin's trace JSON into one static HTML page and a Markdown summary. CI uploads the page as the test-report artifact and appends the summary to the run page.

Reason. ADR 045's ladder: the input formats are the ecosystem's own, and no framework or community tool joins test results to specification rules and to a function inventory, which is the view ADR 049 R3 asks for. The generator is a few hundred lines with the standard library only.

Alternatives. Allure Report: a polished viewer, but it needs its Java CLI, and the per-rule and per-function gap view would still be ours to build as labels and post-processing. pytest-html: one page of test results, nothing about rules or functions. SonarCloud: shows coverage, not traceability.

Consequences. The page is an artifact of the CI run, not a published site; 0.4 adds the parity results to it. If a later need (history, trends) outgrows a static page, a viewer is chosen then.

items.title: DD-012. Parity scenarios are YAML files run as parametrised pytest tests
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.4
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. A scenario is a *.scenario.yaml file in the stage shape of Tavern (request, response, save), validated with pydantic. A project's test module turns a directory of them into one parametrised test, load_scenarios(directory), whose body is await run_scenario(scenario, client); the project's fixture decides whether client talks to the application in-process (httpx.ASGITransport) or over HTTP to a running server.

Reason. ADR 045's ladder: the request/response/save stage is the community's shape for declarative API tests, so reviewers who know Tavern read our scenarios at once. Running scenarios as ordinary pytest parameters puts them in JUnit, in the trace file and under covers (SCN-04) with public pytest API only.

Alternatives. Tavern itself: speaks HTTP through requests only, so the in-process unit level is lost, and the exact comparison, volatile paths and deviations (DD-013) would be hooks around it. A custom collector for *.scenario.yaml: shorter test modules, but it needs pytest's private fixture API to give the items a client. Schemathesis: generates requests from an OpenAPI document, which Atlas 2.4.0 does not ship and which states types, not Atlas's answers.

Consequences. Every project with scenarios has one small test module and a client fixture. The scenario format is ours to keep stable; it is versioned by its rules SCN-01 to SCN-03.

items.title: DD-013. A scenario response is compared exactly, except at declared paths
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.4
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The expected body must equal the actual body: the same keys, arrays in the same order, booleans and null distinct from numbers. Only volatile paths (generated GUIDs, timestamps) skip the value, and only deviations entries change the expectation, each naming its DV-NN.

Reason. The dashboard and existing clients read fields the scenarios might not think of; an extra, missing or null field is a visible difference (ADR 046). Atlas serialises its models with Jackson NON_NULL inclusion, so "absent" and null differ there and must differ here.

Alternatives. Subset matching: short scenarios, but an extra or misnamed field passes. Snapshot files written from our own responses: exact, but the expectation would come from the implementation, not from Atlas (ADR 052 R1).

Consequences. Expectations for large responses are long; scenarios borrow Atlas's own test fixtures for request bodies to keep writing them cheap. Arrays whose order Atlas does not define get an explicit order-insensitive option when the first increment needs one.

items.title: DD-014. Scenario facts reach the report as test properties
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.4
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The parity plugin adds each scenario's endpoints and deviation ids to the test item's user_properties at collection. The trace plugin writes every test's properties to the trace file, so check (unknown deviations) and report (one row per endpoint) read them from the collection they already do.

Reason. user_properties is pytest's own channel for facts about a test, and JUnit carries it too. Reading it at collection keeps the report's rule of DD-009: an endpoint whose scenarios did not run in this change is not run, not missing.

Alternatives. A separate --parity-json file: a second format next to the trace file for the same tests. Make the trace library know scenarios: couples the traceability tool to one kind of test.

Consequences. The trace file format gains a properties field per test; readers of version 1 files without it see no properties. Property names are prefixed with the plugin that sets them (parity.).

items.title: DD-015. The server is a FastAPI application with one router per Atlas resource
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.5
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. apps/aurelius-atlas-server is a FastAPI application built like the template's example service (settings, uvicorn entry point, logfire, hardened image), with one router module per Atlas REST resource class (AdminResource → routes/admin.py, later EntityREST → routes/entity.py). Atlas errors are raised as AtlasError and turned into the Atlas error body by one exception handler, as AtlasBaseExceptionMapper does; JSON goes out as application/json; charset=UTF-8.

Reason. ADR 045's ladder: FastAPI and the example's wiring are the workspace's convention, already gated, observed and packaged. Mirroring the Java resource classes keeps the Java map one row per class and lets a reviewer put a router next to its Java resource.

Alternatives. Starlette without FastAPI: no validation or OpenAPI for the request models later increments need. Routers per URL prefix rather than per Java class: admin would still be one, but /v2/entity and /v2/entity/bulk belong to one Java class and would split.

Consequences. The example service is no longer the only FastAPI app; it stays until the plan is done (DD-019). Later increments add routers and error codes; the error handler and media type stay.

items.title: DD-016. The server does not start without its store
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.5
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The server opens the Elasticsearch store in its start-up and stops with an error when the store cannot be opened (unreachable, rejected, or not Elasticsearch 9). Once running, readiness reports the store's health on every call, and liveness and status do not depend on it.

Reason. The store is the only system of record (ADR 047); a server without it cannot answer anything but the admin endpoints. Failing at start-up shows a wrong setting at once (ADR 018) and lets an orchestrator restart the container, while readiness covers a store that goes away later.

Alternatives. Start without the store and retry in the background: a misconfigured server would run and only its readiness would say so. Make liveness depend on the store: an outage of Elasticsearch would make an orchestrator restart every server, which does not help.

Consequences. Start-up order matters: nx serve and the end-to-end tests start the dev store first.

items.title: DD-017. The dashboards are vendored unchanged and built with dart-sass on Node 24
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.6
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. apps/aurelius-atlas-dashboard/dashboardv2 and dashboardv3 are copies of the release-2.4.0 tag, byte for byte, with Atlas's LICENSE and NOTICE. Every change is a patch listed in PATCHES.md and made in its own commit. The first patch replaces node-sass with sass (dart-sass) in both gruntfile.js files and package.json files. Both dashboards are built with grunt build-minify, as Atlas's Maven build does, in the hardened Node 24 image; only the built files leave the build. The workspace's formatters, linters and hooks skip the vendored directories.

Reason. DD-001 asks for the dashboards unchanged; a vendored copy lets a reviewer prove that with a diff against the tag. node-sass 9 is a native module with builds for Node 16 to 20 only, and Node 20 is past its end of life; dart-sass is pure JavaScript, the maintained Sass compiler, and grunt-sass supports it. A trial build on Node 24 gave the same files as Atlas's toolchain on Node 20, with identical JavaScript; only the two compiled stylesheets differ.

Alternatives. Build unchanged on Node 20: no patch, but an unsupported Node and a native compile in every build. Download the tag at build time and apply patch files: a smaller repository, but the source the build uses is not in review. Commit the built files: no legacy toolchain at all, but the shipped files cannot be reviewed or rebuilt.

Consequences. The vendored package-lock.json files keep their 2020-era dependencies; they only run inside the build container and are not part of the server image, so Dependabot does not watch them. Moving to another Atlas release replaces both directories and re-applies PATCHES.md.

items.title: DD-018. The server serves the dashboards from the API's origin
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.6
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The server mounts the built dashboardv3 at /n/ and dashboardv2 at / as static files, after the API routes, when AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_DASHBOARD_DIR names their directory. The server image contains the built dashboards and sets that setting.

Reason. The dashboards call api/atlas/... with relative URLs and rely on the session cookie of the same origin, as in Atlas's web application. Serving them from the server keeps that without a proxy or cross-origin configuration, and one image is the whole product.

Alternatives. A separate static file server or the template's Angular serving: a second container and a proxy to keep one origin. Serving through a CDN: possible later in front of the server; nothing here prevents it.

Consequences. API paths must never collide with dashboard files; the API is matched first. Unit tests build their settings without the environment and serve no dashboards unless a test sets the directory; nx serve builds the dashboards first and its .env points at dist/.

items.title: DD-019. The template examples stay until the plan is done
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 0.6
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The removal of the template's examples, planned as increment 0.7, moves to a to-do after 6.4. Until then, the FastAPI example service, the Angular example screen and its libraries, aurelius-atlas-example, aurelius-atlas-sdk and dev/postgres stay in the workspace. They remain the named deviation of ADR 050.

Reason. The project's second phase needs these components again. Removing them now and restoring them from the template later would cost more than keeping them.

Alternatives. Remove them now, as ADR 050 plans once the server and the dashboards replace them: this fulfils ADR 050's R1 sooner, but the components would have to be restored for the second phase.

Consequences. CI keeps building, testing and scanning the examples. 1.1 follows 0.6 directly. The to-do in the roadmap records the scope already agreed for the removal: everything the catalogue does not use, apart from dev/keycloak.

items.title: DD-020. Typedef models are Pydantic models that read and write Atlas's JSON
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.1
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. Each Atlas typedef class is a Pydantic model in aurelius_atlas_model.typedef with snake_case attributes and the Java getter names as aliases. model_validate reads a request body and to_json writes a response body: aliases, null fields left out, empty collections kept. Unknown fields are ignored. The Java setters' normalisations run as _-prefixed validators, so they apply when a body is read and when a model is built in code, as the Java constructors and setters do.

Reason. Pydantic is already the workspace's modelling library (settings, store) and FastAPI reads and writes it natively, so 1.6 needs no mapping layer. Atlas writes with Jackson NON_NULL, which is Pydantic's exclude_none; empty collections stay because Jackson keeps them (DD-013 compares exactly).

Alternatives. Dataclasses with a hand-written JSON codec: no dependency, but every rule of TDM-01 to TDM-15 would be custom code. Generating models from Atlas's JSON schema: Atlas publishes none, and the normalisations live in Java setters a schema cannot express.

Consequences. Response bodies must be written with to_json (or its exclude_none, by_alias dump), never with FastAPI's default response model serialisation. Later model packages (entities in 2.1) follow the same pattern.

items.title: DD-021. Set-valued fields keep each name once, in first-seen order
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.1
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. superTypes, subTypes and entityTypes are lists without duplicates, kept in the order the names were first given.

Reason. Java holds them in a HashSet and writes them in hash order, which Atlas does not define and no client can rely on. A Python set would make our order vary from run to run; first-seen order is stable and keeps what the client sent.

Alternatives. Reproduce Java's HashSet iteration order: possible from String.hashCode and the table size, but it would copy an accident of the implementation. Sorted order: stable, but reorders what clients send.

Consequences. The JSON order of these arrays can differ from Atlas's. Parity scenarios compare them without order, through the option DD-013 foresees, which 1.6 adds with the first scenario that needs it.

items.title: DD-022. Typedef timestamps are aware datetimes, written as epoch milliseconds
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.1
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. createTime and updateTime are timezone-aware UTC datetimes. They are written as integer milliseconds since the epoch and read from a number, a string of digits or an ISO-8601 date-time string.

Reason. Atlas's REST mapper has no date serialiser, so Jackson writes java.util.Date as epoch milliseconds and its StdDateFormat reads numbers, digit strings and ISO-8601. Pydantic would read a bare integer as seconds or milliseconds depending on its size, so the conversion is explicit.

Alternatives. Keep the raw integer: exact, but every caller would convert. Write ISO-8601 strings: readable, but a visible difference from Atlas.

Consequences. Jackson's RFC 1123 form (Tue, 17 Oct 2026 10:00:00 GMT) is not read. No Atlas client is known to send it; if one does, it becomes a deviation.

items.title: DD-023. Atlas errors live in the model library
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. AtlasErrorCode and AtlasError move from aurelius_atlas_server.errors to aurelius_atlas_model.errors. Each code keeps Atlas's HTTP status, error code and message template. The server keeps the error handler and the response class and imports the errors from there.

Reason. The type system (1.2) and the stores raise Atlas errors, and they may not depend on the server (DD-002: model ← typesystem ← core; server → core). In Java, too, AtlasErrorCode sits in intg, below everything else.

Alternatives. A separate errors library: one more project for two classes. Each layer with its own exception, mapped in the server: the mapping would repeat Atlas's error table.

Consequences. New error codes are added to aurelius_atlas_model.errors as each increment needs them, copied from AtlasErrorCode.

items.title: DD-024. The registry is updated on a transient copy under a re-entrant lock
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. TypeRegistry.lock_for_update(timeout) returns a TransientTypeRegistry built from the registry's definitions, under a re-entrant threading.RLock. Changes resolve every type on the copy; release(transient, commit=...) swaps the copy's types into the registry or drops them. A context manager wraps the pair.

Reason. It is Atlas's TypeRegistryUpdateSynchronizer: readers never see a half-resolved registry, and a failed change leaves the registry as it was (TRG-05, TRG-09). A thread lock also protects FastAPI's thread-pool handlers; async handlers hold it only around synchronous code.

Alternatives. An asyncio.Lock: does not protect code run in threads. Copy-on-write without a lock: two concurrent updates would each start from the same registry and one would be lost.

Consequences. The lock is per process. Several server processes keep their registries in step through the store (1.4).

items.title: DD-025. The type system ports the definition side only
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.2
  • Date: 2026-10-17

Decision. The ported types resolve definitions: names, attribute types, cardinalities, constraints and later the hierarchies (1.3). Their value side (isValidValue, getNormalizedValue, validateValue, createDefaultValue, areEqualValues) is ported with entity validation in 2.1. Their JanusGraph side (vertex property names, unique property names, index field names, index-query escaping) is not ported.

Reason. Types REST (1.6) needs only the definition side; values first matter for entities (2.1), which is where Atlas's tests for them can be run. The JanusGraph names have no meaning in Elasticsearch: the index mapping is designed in 2.2.

Alternatives. Port each class whole: one increment several times the size limit, with value code untested by any endpoint until 2.x.

Consequences. The type classes grow in 2.1. Atlas behaviour that depends on vertex property names is designed again for Elasticsearch in 2.2 and recorded there.

items.title: DD-026. Dynamic attributes and search lookups wait for their increments
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.3
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. The entity type's dynamic attributes (dynAttribute: templates, their parsing and evaluation order) are ported with entity writes in 2.4. The root entity type's lookup of business attributes for search is ported with basic search in 4.1. Both resolve nothing a type definition is checked against.

Reason. They are used only when entities are written or searched, and can only be tested there; porting them now would leave them untested by any endpoint until then (as DD-025 argues for values).

Alternatives. Port them with the rest of AtlasEntityType now: a larger increment whose extra code no rule of 1.3 can exercise.

Consequences. 2.4 adds the template parsing to EntityType; 4.1 adds the lookup to the root type.

items.title: DD-027. Derived type sets keep first-seen order
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.3
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. All super types are listed in the order the depth-first walk of the super types first reaches them; sub types and relationship attributes in the order the registry resolves its types, which is the order the definitions were added in.

Reason. Java keeps them in HashSets and HashMaps, whose order Atlas does not define; first-seen order is stable, as for the definitions' own sets (DD-021). Where the order picks a winner, as for inherited relationship attributes, Java's winner is equally arbitrary.

Alternatives. Sort them by name: stable too, but unrelated to how the hierarchy was declared.

Consequences. subTypes in responses may be ordered differently from Atlas's; parity scenarios compare them without order (DD-021, from 1.6).

items.title: DD-028. The type definitions are one Elasticsearch document
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.4
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. All stored type definitions are one document, typedefs, in the index aurelius-atlas-typedefs (through an alias, so a reindex can swap it). The document holds the definitions in their stored form (TDS-05, TDS-06), grouped by kind as in AtlasTypesDef. Every change replaces the whole document, guarded by if_seq_no and if_primary_term.

Reason. Atlas changes several definitions in one graph transaction: createTypesDef stores all of a request or none (TDS-10). Elasticsearch has no transaction across documents, but writes one document atomically, so one document makes every typedef change atomic and its sequence number a single version of all types (DD-029). The registry, not Elasticsearch, answers every query over types; the document is read whole at start-up and on change. Atlas's built-in models with all patches are about 1 MB of JSON, well inside Elasticsearch's limits.

Alternatives. One document per definition, keyed by name: queryable, and a create can use op_type=create for uniqueness, but a request touching several definitions needs a hand-written rollback when one write fails, and other processes see half a change. A changes log of operations, replayed at start-up: atomic per entry, but every process replays the whole history and compaction is extra work.

Consequences. The document's size grows with the number of types; a deployment with tens of thousands of custom types would revisit this. Type changes are serialised across the cluster, as Atlas serialises them with its update lock.

items.title: DD-029. Server processes share the type definitions through the document's version
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.4
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. Each process remembers the _seq_no and _primary_term of the typedefs document its registry was built from. Before a type change it reloads when the stored document is newer; it then writes conditionally on what it read. A conflict means another process changed types first: the process reloads, applies the change again on the new definitions, and gives up with FAILED_TO_OBTAIN_TYPE_UPDATE_LOCK after a second conflict. Readers reload when the document changed, checked at most every AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_TYPEDEF_REFRESH_SECONDS (default 5).

Reason. Atlas runs one active server and keeps its registry in memory (DD-024 is per process). Several processes behind a load balancer must not lose each other's changes, and a change must reach the others without a restart. Optimistic concurrency on one document gives both with one cheap GET of the document's version.

Alternatives. A lock document: needs expiry and recovery when its holder dies. Change notification through a message bus: a component the system does not have (ADR 050).

Consequences. For up to the refresh interval, a process may answer from older types than another; a type change is visible at once only on the process that made it. 6.4 measures whether the interval needs tuning.

items.title: DD-030. The store asks the entity store whether a type is in use
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.4
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. The typedef store takes a TypeUsage callback that answers whether entities, classifications or relationships of a type exist; deleting a type that is in use fails with TYPE_HAS_REFERENCES. Until the entity store exists (2.2) the callback answers "not in use".

Reason. Atlas checks typeHasInstanceVertex before deleting a type. The instances live in the entity store, which the typedef store must not depend on; a callback keeps the dependency pointing from core's entity store to the typedef store.

Alternatives. Query the entity index from the typedef store: couples it to an index that does not exist yet.

Consequences. 2.2 passes its own check when it builds the stores.

items.title: DD-031. The patch records live in the typedef document
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Increment: 1.5
  • Date: 2026-10-18

Decision. The typedefs document of DD-028 holds, next to typesDef, a list patches of AtlasPatch records: one per typedef patch id, with its description, type, action, status and times. A patch's record is written in the same document write as the type change it makes.

Reason. Atlas keeps patch records as graph vertices and commits them after the type change, so a crash between the two applies a patch twice, which the typeVersion check mostly hides. One document makes the change and its record atomic, and gives both the single version of DD-029: a process that loses a race reloads the records with the types, and sees the patch as already applied (MDL-15).
