items.title: Increment 8.4 — API client libraries
items.text: Field Value Status in progress Author Aurelius Atlas maintainers Date 2026-10-23 ADRs 051 (increments), 049 (traceability), 055 (auxiliary APIs are a named data surface), 036 (per-app OTel exporter chain — unchanged), 050 (the template's example apps are removed, not served here) Design log DD-203 (the contract lives in a client library; the app imports it), DD-204 (clients are async httpx, superseded on construction by DD-205), DD-205 (the httpx.AsyncClient is provided externally)

items.title: Objective
items.text:
Every Python HTTP API in the workspace answers a wire contract today — the server's Atlas REST routes, data2model's /extract, lineage-model's GET /, and validate-entity's POST / — and every one of them states that contract inside the app that serves it, or not at all (the server answers .to_json() dicts, data2model answers an untyped dict, validate-entity answers a dict constant). There is no Python client anywhere: aurelius-atlas-sdk is utility code, and the only outbound calls (lineage-model's upstreams) are ad-hoc httpx.

This increment gives each API an accompanying library that owns the contract — pydantic models for the requests and responses — and an API client for it. The Angular side has this shape already (libs/angular/aurelius-atlas-data-access, 7.3); this is its Python twin. The apps stop being the sole definition site of their own wire contract: each imports the models its client library states, so a consumer and the server validate against one source of truth (DD-203).

Four libraries, one per API:

Library Contract Client libs/python/aurelius-atlas-server-client the Atlas metadata API the server routes answer (admin, types), plus the Atlas lineage body v2/lineage/{guid} AtlasClient libs/python/aurelius-atlas-data2model-client POST /extract: the rules document in, {model, metadata} out Data2ModelClient libs/python/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model-client GET /?guid=&depth=&direction= of 8.2 LineageModelClient libs/python/aurelius-atlas-validate-entity-client POST / of 8.3: the governance-quality document out ValidateEntityClient

items.title: Scope
items.text:
In scope:

  • The four libraries, scaffolded per libs/python/AGENTS.md and registered in the root pyproject.toml.
  • The relocation of each contract's models into its client library (DD-203): ExtractionRequest and the rule-model family out of aurelius_atlas_data2model.rules; LineageInfo, EntityHeaderLite, LineageRelation and Direction out of aurelius_atlas_lineage_model.lineage; and the new response models the apps never had (ExtractionResponse, ValidationResponse, the admin shapes).
  • The four async clients, on the shared client conventions (CL-01..CL-07).
  • The apps rewired to import their own contract and, for lineage-model, to call its upstreams through the clients (its routes become async def).
  • Unit tests for every public function (covers, ADR 049), mkdocstrings pages.

Out of scope:

  • aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example — a template demo, removed by ADR 050; it keeps its in-app Envelope/PaginatedResponse models.
  • AtlasClient.get_lineage — the method lands with the server's lineage feed (5.1), spec-first; only the lineage models move here, because 8.2 consumes them.
  • Entity/search/discovery server routes (increments 2.x–6.x) — each adds its client methods and DTOs as it ships the route, the pattern this increment sets.
  • The Angular data-access lib (stays hand-mirrored) and a code generator (openapi → pydantic): hand-written, reviewable contracts, parity-guarded (ADR 052).
  • Real governance validation (DV-67) and the auth/otel libs (8.0).

items.title: Semantics
items.text: Each rule the behaviour must obey, with an id that tests name in @pytest.mark.covers(..., rules=["CL-NN"]).

items.title: The client libraries (all four)
items.text: Id Rule CL-01 A client is constructed from an externally provided httpx.AsyncClient and a token source, and reads no environment variables — the app builds the httpx client from its own settings (TLS, timeout) and passes it in. The client's request paths are relative to that client's base URL, so the app's URL passes through as given — a pydantic HttpUrl's str(), which ends in a trailing slash, needs no trimming (the libs-python rule, as aurelius-atlas-auth). CL-02 The httpx.AsyncClient a client wraps is provided externally, so tests pass one built on a MockTransport and no socket opens (the DD-200 seam, made async); whoever builds the httpx client closes it — the API client exposes no close of its own, it borrows the pool, and a with_token wrapper shares it and closes nothing. CL-03 Every request carries authorization: Bearer <token> from the token source, on every call — the browser-token-forwarding of 8.2 is one source (a callable yielding the caller's token), not a special case. An empty token is the unauthenticated call: no header at all — an empty bearer is not a legal HTTP header value, and the server's open routes (6.1 closes them) must be reachable with an empty source. CL-04 A non-2xx answer raises the library's *ClientError carrying the status and, when the body parses, the server's {errorCode, errorMessage}; a success raises nothing. A 204 on a lineage-model call is the caller's success path, not an error. CL-05 An unreachable upstream (httpx.RequestError) propagates as httpx's own error — mapping a transport failure to an HTTP status is the app's job (LM-07's DV-80), not the client's. CL-06 The models are the wire contract: camelCase field aliases on Atlas-shaped bodies (typeName, guidEntityMap), extra="ignore" on what the apps read leniently, and the legacy None-to-'' normalisation where DTM-11 states it. CL-07 An app imports its own request/response models from its client library — the library is the contract's single home, and both sides of every in-workspace call validate against one model class.

items.title: Per-library contracts
items.text: Id Rule CL-10 aurelius_atlas_server_client.models states the admin shapes as models — AtlasVersion (Version/Revision/Name/Description), AtlasStatus (Status), AtlasSessionInfo (settings keys + userName/groups/timezones/_csrfToken), AtlasErrorInfo (errorCode/errorMessage/errorCause) — reusing aurelius-atlas-model for typedef bodies, which it never forks. CL-11 AtlasClient answers the server's implemented routes: admin.version(), admin.status(), admin.session(), admin.readiness(), liveness(); the typedef calls typedef_by_name, typedef_by_guid, typedefs(filter), typedef_headers(filter), the six kind lookups (enumdef…businessmetadatadef, by name and guid), and the create/update/delete writes — each path mirroring routes/admin.py / routes/types.py. get_lineage(guid, depth, direction) -> LineageInfo reads v2/lineage/{guid} (CL-12's model; the guid is a UUID — DV-78, DD-213) — the client side of the feed whose server route lands with 5.1; 8.2 is its first caller. CL-12 aurelius_atlas_server_client.lineage owns the v2/lineage/{guid} body — LineageInfo, EntityHeaderLite, LineageRelation, Direction — moved verbatim from 8.2's app module (LM-04's model, LM-01's Direction), the entity guids typed as UUID (guidEntityMap keys, headers, relation endpoints — DV-78; relationshipId stays str); the flattening (flatten_relations, PROCESS_TYPES, LINEAGE_RULES) is 8.2's app logic and stays in the app. CL-20 aurelius_atlas_data2model_client owns the /extract contract: the rule-model family (ExtractionRequest, RulesDef, ElementRule, RelationRule, ViewRule, ViewNodeRule, ViewEdgeRule, MappingEntry, LegacyStr, the DTM-11 validation messages) moved out of the app, and the new ExtractionResponse (metadata: list[MetadataEntry], model: str — the ar3 JSON string). CL-21 Data2ModelClient.extract(request) posts an ExtractionRequest and returns an ExtractionResponse; the rules document the 8.2 chain sends is built from the lib's rule models, so the caller's payload validates as the server's body. CL-30 aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client states GET / (8.2): LineageModelParams (guid — a UUID, DV-78 — depth ≥ 1 default 3, direction, the LM-01 shape) and LineageModelResponse (the {model, metadata} passthrough of /extract, LM-04); LineageModelClient.get(guid, depth, direction) maps a 204 to None (LM-05/LM-06's empty answer). CL-40 aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client states POST / (8.3): ValidationResponse — the four governance cards (dataEntity/definition/domainLead/name, each items + isNonCompliant) as the browser's GovQualityApi consumes them (VE-02); validate(entity) posts any mapping — the body is not a model, because the mock never reads it (VE-01, DD-201).

items.title: Wiring rules
items.text: Id Rule CL-50 Each app's create_app keeps its injectable seams; the upstream clients of 8.2 inject there (the http= seam becomes typed clients, DD-200). A client library's models cross the app boundary: the app validates its request body with the library's model, the library's client parses the response into the library's model, and the app's response bytes stay verbatim (no response_model filtering — 8.1's scenarios compare whole bodies; the response model states the contract the server's own tests assert against).

items.title: Aurelius origin
items.text:
The reference is the Aurelius source (ADR 055 R4) and this workspace's own routes:

  • libs/atlas/api (TypeDefsService, AdminService, DTOs) — the Angular client this is the Python twin of; the DTO names and endpoint paths match it.
  • backend/m4i-data2model (extract endpoint: {metadata, model}), backend/m4i-lineage-model (lineage_model.py: the rules dict, the fetch/extract chain), backend/m4i-validate-entity (mock_response, the output dict).
  • libs/m4i-atlas-core's LineageInfo (the camelCase wire shape now owned here).
  • This workspace: apps/aurelius-atlas-server/aurelius_atlas_server/routes/{admin,types}.py and errors.py (the admin/types paths and the {errorCode, errorMessage} body the client mirrors), and the 8.1–8.3 specs for the aux-API contracts.

items.title: Deviations
items.text: None of Atlas (ADR 052 — the wire contracts are unchanged; 8.1–8.3's DVs stand). Deliberate workspace decisions, recorded as DD-203 (the contract's home), DD-204 (async client, no env — superseded on construction by DD-205) and DD-205 (the httpx.AsyncClient is provided externally) in the design log — this increment adds no DV- rows because it changes no wire behaviour.

items.title: Data contracts
items.text:
• aurelius_atlas_server_client: AtlasClient(http, token) (http an externally built httpx.AsyncClient), .admin (version() -> AtlasVersion, status() -> AtlasStatus, session() -> AtlasSessionInfo, readiness() -> str, liveness() -> str), .types (typedef_by_name(name) -> AtlasBaseTypeDef, typedef_by_guid(guid), typedefs(params) -> AtlasTypesDef, typedef_headers(params) -> list[AtlasTypeDefHeader], enumdef_by_name(name) -> AtlasEnumDef … businessmetadatadef_by_guid(guid), create_typedefs(AtlasTypesDef) -> AtlasTypesDef, update_typedefs(...), delete_typedefs(...) -> None, delete_typedef_by_name(name) -> None), lineage.LineageInfo (+EntityHeaderLite, LineageRelation, Direction), models.AtlasErrorInfo, AtlasClientError.
  • aurelius_atlas_data2model_client: the rule-model family (CL-20) at the package root, ExtractionResponse, Data2ModelClient(http, token).extract(request) -> ExtractionResponse, Data2ModelClientError.
  • aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client: LineageModelParams, LineageModelResponse, LineageModelClient(http, token).get(guid: UUID, depth=3, direction="BOTH") -> LineageModelResponse | None, LineageModelClientError.
  • aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client: ValidationResponse (+card/item models), ValidateEntityClient(http, token).validate(entity: Mapping) -> ValidationResponse, ValidateEntityClientError.
  • Apps: aurelius_atlas_data2model.rules re-exports its family from the client lib (a thin compatibility module, so the app's docstrings keep citing DTM rules); aurelius_atlas_lineage_model.lineage keeps PROCESS_TYPES, LINEAGE_RULES, flatten_relations, UpstreamError and imports the models from aurelius_atlas_server_client.lineage; create_app(settings, auth=None, atlas=None, d2m=None).

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
• Unit (per lib, every public function named by covers with a CL id; basenames unique across the workspace, the pytest convention): libs/python/aurelius-atlas-server-client/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_server_client_models.py (CL-10), test__aurelius_atlas_server_client_lineage.py (CL-12), test__aurelius_atlas_server_client_client.py (CL-01..05, CL-11), libs/python/aurelius-atlas-data2model-client/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_data2model_client_models.py (CL-20), test__aurelius_atlas_data2model_client_client.py (CL-01..04, CL-21), libs/python/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model-client/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client_models.py (CL-30), test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client_client.py, libs/python/aurelius-atlas-validate-entity-client/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client_models.py (CL-40), test__aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_client_client.py; CL-06/CL-07/CL-50 are enforced by the apps' suites (importing the lib's models) and the client suites' transport fakes.
  • The apps' suites stay green unchanged in behaviour: the 8.1/8.2/8.3 unit suites prove no wire change. The e2e suites (nx e2e aurelius-atlas-{data2model,lineage-model,validate-entity,server}) drive the containers through the client libraries — each conftest's api fixture wraps a CA-verified httpx.AsyncClient in the app's client (CL-21, CL-30, CL-40, CL-11), so the libraries are proven against the real apps, not only a fake transport. The raw-httpx fixtures stay where the library has no route: the parity scenarios (run_scenario takes httpx.AsyncClient), the auth-gate 401s, liveness, and the malformed-body call of VE-01.
  • uv run aurelius-atlas-trace check names every public function (CL ids resolve).
  • Parity: none added — no wire behaviour changes; the existing server scenarios (scenarios/*.scenario.yaml) and 8.1–8.3 scenarios are the guard.

Run: uv run pytest libs/python/aurelius-atlas-{server,data2model,lineage,validate-entity}*-client* and the app suites; CI gate nx affected -t test e2e -c ci.

items.title: Increment 8.5 — lineage-model circuit breakers
items.text: Field Value Status in progress Author Aurelius Atlas maintainers Date 2026-10-23 ADRs 051 (increments), 049 (traceability), 055 (auxiliary APIs are a named data surface), 037 (the system promises nothing about staying up) Design log DD-197 (foundation), DD-200 (proxy app), DD-205 (clients provided externally), DD-206 (the breakers live in the app, on the calling() seam), DD-207 (the app's provider/route layout), DD-208 (the flow lives in the route)

items.title: Objective
items.text:
The 8.2 app forwards every request to two upstreams — the Atlas v2/lineage feed and the 8.1 data2model /extract — and when an upstream is down, every request pays for it: a full connect/timeout attempt, on the app's pool, for every caller, forever. LM-07 answers those calls 502 (DV-80), which is honest but not protective.

Guard each upstream with a circuit breaker (pybreaker, the workspace's existing breaker — the auth library puts one in front of the JWKS fetch, AUX-02): after a run of upstream outages the circuit opens and further calls fail fast with the same 502, without reaching the upstream; after a reset timeout, one trial call probes the upstream, and success closes the circuit.

The breaker is the app's resilience policy, not the wire contract: the client libraries of 8.4 stay transport-only (DD-205), and the response bytes, the auth gate, and the LM-01..LM-10 rules are unchanged.

items.title: Scope
items.text:
In scope: two per-upstream breakers in apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model (the Atlas feed, the data2model extract), the open-circuit answer, the outage/fact counting policy, the two settings, unit tests.

Out of scope: breakers in the client libraries (DD-205 keeps them transport-only — a breaker is the caller's policy, and each caller owns its policy); breakers in the other aux apps (8.1 and 8.3 have no upstreams); bulkheads/rate limits/retries (the pool cap is DD-200's, retries are a 6.x platform topic); per-endpoint metrics for the breaker state (the listener logs state changes — a metric leg rides with the otel increments).

items.title: Contracts and Rules
items.text: The reference is the Aurelius source (ADR 055 R4): backend/m4i-lineage-model/m4i_lineage_model/lineage_model.py calls requests.post bare — no breaker, no retries; the legacy has no breaker behaviour to port, so the rules below state the workspace convention (the auth library's JWKS breaker, AUX-02) applied to the 8.2 chain. DV-77.

items.title: The upstream circuit breakers
items.text:
Id Rule LM-11 The app guards each upstream with its own circuit breaker (pybreaker): the Atlas lineage fetch and the data2model extract are counted separately, so one failing upstream never fast-fails calls bound for the healthy one (the 204 of LM-05 must keep flowing past a dead data2model). The breakers are built from the settings by the app's upstream factory (providers/upstreams.py, DD-207, DD-208) and exposed on app.state, guarding the route's calls. LM-12 A circuit that is open answers 502 with the Atlas error body (the LM-07 family) without calling the upstream — the fast-fail is the point: no pool connection, no timeout, for every request that arrives while the circuit is open. LM-13 Only outages count towards opening a circuit: an upstream 5xx (AtlasClientError/Data2ModelClientError with status ≥ 500) and a transport failure (httpx.RequestError). An upstream 4xx is a fact, not an outage — the 404 of LM-05 (answered 204) and the 400 of LM-07 (the caller's own guid) reset the failure counter, exactly as the auth library treats a 4xx from the issuer (AUX-02). LM-14 After the reset timeout, the next call is the half-open trial: it reaches the upstream; success closes the circuit and answers normally, a failure re-opens it and answers 502 (LM-12). The trial is one call, not a probe schedule. LM-15 Settings (same prefix, LM-10): breaker_fail_max (default 5, ≥ 1) is the outages that open a circuit, breaker_reset_timeout (default 60 s, > 0) is how long it stays open — the same shape and defaults as the auth library's issuer breaker (AuthConfig.fail_max/reset_timeout).

The app's behaviour for closed circuits is unchanged: LM-01 (verbatim answer), LM-05 (404 → 204), LM-07 (5xx/unreachable → 502), LM-08 (auth gate), LM-09 (liveness) stand as specified in 8.2. The open-circuit 502 is the same wire shape DV-80 defines, with a message naming the fast-fail.

items.title: Aurelius origin
items.text: The legacy m4i-lineage-model (Flask, requests.post to data2model, m4i-atlas-core.get_lineage_by_guid) has no resilience device — its dev aiocache @cached() is not ported (8.2). The breaker is new behaviour, recorded as DV-77; the workspace convention it follows is aurelius-atlas-auth's JWKS breaker (AUX-02, same pybreaker dependency).

items.title: Deviations
items.text:
DV-77 (deviations.md): the legacy has no upstream circuit breaker; the port guards each upstream with one, opening on 5xx/transport failures only. Technical decisions in DD-206 (design-log.md): the breakers live in the app (not the client libraries — DD-205 keeps the libs transport-only); one breaker per upstream; the pybreaker calling() generator seam is the async-safe form (the lib's call_async is tornado-only and fails on this Python); the exclude predicate counts 4xx as facts.

DV-78 (deviations.md, DD-213 — rides this branch, not this spec's breakers): the lineage chain's guid is a UUID on every typed surface; a non-UUID guid is LM-07's 400 before any upstream call, so a malformed guid never reaches the guarded fetch.

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
• Unit (the 8.2 app suite, fake upstream + recording transport): tests/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_app.py — test__the_app_carries_one_breaker_per_upstream (LM-11, LM-15), test__the_upstream_outages_open_the_circuit (LM-11, LM-13), test__an_open_circuit_answers_without_calling_the_upstream (LM-12), test__a_dead_atlas_circuit_leaves_the_extract_circuit_closed (LM-11, LM-12), test__an_upstream_4xx_is_a_fact_not_an_outage (LM-13), test__the_half_open_trial_closes_the_circuit_on_success (LM-14), test__the_half_open_trial_reopens_the_circuit_on_failure (LM-14); tests/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_settings.py — test__the_breaker_settings_have_the_auth_shape (LM-15); tests/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_providers_upstreams.py — test__the_breakers_are_per_upstream_and_take_the_settings (LM-11, LM-15), test__an_upstream_4xx_is_a_fact_everything_else_is_not (LM-13). Every transport here is a mock, so the half-open trial is driven through pybreaker's management API (half_open()) — the wall-clock reset is the library's own tested behaviour, not slept through.
  • The 8.2 e2e chain stays green unchanged: a healthy chain never opens a circuit (closed circuits are byte-identical to 8.2), and the e2e fixture Atlas is a static file server, so the open path is proven at unit level.
  • uv run aurelius-atlas-trace check names every public function (LM ids resolve).
  • Parity: none added — no wire behaviour changes on the closed path; the 8.2 scenario is the guard.

Run: uv run pytest apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model/tests and nx e2e aurelius-atlas-lineage-model.

items.title: 8.6 Aux API failure hardening
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: — (follows the review of 2026-10-24, DD-214)
  • Records: DD-214 (the review that scoped this); cites 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5, ADR 052

items.title: Scope
items.text:
Test-completeness, not new semantics: the review found the aux APIs' failure behaviours already specified (DTM-04/06/07, LM-07/11/12/13, VE-01) with unproven paths. This increment closes the proof gaps in the three auxiliary apps:

  • data2model — the extraction engine's view-edge selection, dynamic views, dynamic view names, the archimate_hierarchical layout, and relation-level id dedupe (all at 0% line coverage).
  • lineage-model — the transport-failure handler (app.py, LM-07/DV-80), the data2model-side open-circuit fast-fail (LM-12), and the upstream timeout (LM-13's outage class) — the app's two uncovered lines.
  • validate-entity — the mock's method misuse (405) and oversized body.
  • All three — negative parity scenarios: 400/401 stages in YAML, which the per-app scenario files (all happy-path today) run against both the in-process app and the container, per ADR 052.

It does not deliver: the server's mid-request store failure (deferred backlog #1, DD-214 — the 2.x track's), new client-library behaviour (8.7), frontend UX (7.19), container-stopping e2e (9.1).

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
No new rule ids (DD-214): every behaviour below is already specified by the cited rule, in the cited increment's spec. This table restates the exact path each test pins, so the test names are auditable against the originals.

  • DTM-04 (8-1): a relation rule's duplicate id_key yields one edge/metadata entry — keep-first at the relation level.
  • DTM-06 (8-1): a dynamic view groups rows by id_key (null keys skipped); a dynamic view name reads view_name_key, view_name_prefix, and the legacy 'nan' when the group's key column is absent (DV-70); archimate_hierarchical lays out bottom-to-top.
  • DTM-07 (8-1): a view's view_edges rules select edge ids from the relation's id_key column: model-edge intersection, dedupe in first-seen order, absent-column skip, null-value skip; the selection then filters the between-nodes edges.
  • LM-07 (8-2): a transport failure from an upstream (httpx.RequestError — connect refused, DNS) is answered 502 with the Atlas body, DV-80. An upstream timeout is such a transport failure: a hanging upstream past UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS answers 502, not a hang (LM-10).
  • LM-12 (8-5): the data2model circuit, once open, answers 502 with FAST_FAIL_D2M without calling the extract upstream — the mirror of the proven Atlas-side fast-fail.
  • LM-13 (8-5): a transport failure counts as an outage for its breaker: repeated connect failures open the circuit.
  • VE-01 (8-3): the mock accepts an oversized body and a body with no content-type verbatim — the body is never read (DV-67).
  • (framework default, no rule id): GET / on validate-entity's mock route answers 405 — the legacy is POST-only (DV-67) and there is no GET parity; the test names the route function for ADR 049.

items.title: Java origin
items.text: None new: this increment proves rules whose Java origin 8.1/8.2/8.3/8.5 already cite (data2model's extract.py/to_JSON.py, lineage_model's lineage_model.py, the legacy validation mock). The negative parity stages cite the same legacy sources as their positive counterparts, with the deviation refs the rules carry (DV-70, DV-79, DV-73, DV-75).

items.title: Deviations
items.text: None new. The negative scenarios state existing deviations, each with its deviations: ref in the YAML (the 8.0 harness's feature, DV-06): DV-79 (malformed body → 400, not the legacy Flask 500), DV-73 (a malformed/missing query → 400, not the legacy's int()/Enum() crash 500), DV-67 (any body accepted), DV-70 (null view name renders 'nan' as the legacy does).

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
Unit (naming rules per ADR 049; run uv run pytest apps/<app>/tests):

  • apps/aurelius-atlas-data2model/tests/test__extract.py — appended tests: test__a_relation_id_seen_twice_yields_one_edge (DTM-04), test__view_edges_select_their_rule_column_of_the_model_edges (DTM-07), test__a_view_without_edge_rules_holds_every_edge_between_its_nodes (DTM-07), test__view_edge_selection_skips_a_null_value (DTM-07), test__a_view_edge_rule_for_an_absent_column_is_skipped (DTM-07), test__a_dynamic_view_groups_rows_by_its_key_column (DTM-06), test__a_dynamic_view_name_comes_from_its_key_column (DTM-06), test__a_dynamic_view_name_without_its_key_column_is_the_legacy_nan (DTM-06, DV-70), test__the_hierarchical_layout_ranks_bottom_to_top (DTM-06, DTM-08).
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_app.py — appended tests (the FakeUpstream handler seam, DD-200): test__an_unreachable_atlas_is_a_502_not_a_crash (LM-07, DV-80), test__an_unreachable_extract_is_a_502 (LM-07, DV-80), test__a_dead_extract_circuit_fast_fails_without_calling (LM-12), test__transport_failures_open_the_circuit (LM-13), test__a_hanging_upstream_times_out_to_a_502 (LM-07, LM-10).
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-validate-entity/tests/test__aurelius_atlas_validate_entity_app.py — appended: test__the_mock_route_is_post_only (405), test__a_megabyte_body_still_answers_the_mock (VE-01, DV-67), test__a_body_without_a_content_type_still_answers_the_mock (VE-01, DV-67).

Parity scenarios (ADR 052; run in-process by tests/test__*_scenarios.py and against the container by e2e/*_scenarios_e2e.py):

  • apps/aurelius-atlas-data2model/scenarios/lineage/extract-rejections.scenario.yaml — a malformed body ({"data": "not rows"}) → 400 Atlas body (deviations: [DV-79], cites the legacy extract view's ValueError), and an unknown concept_type rule → 400 (DTM-11).
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model/scenarios/lineage/graph-rejections.scenario.yaml — a missing guid → 400 (deviations: [DV-73], cites the legacy guid None crash), a depth=0 → 400 (DV-73), a direction=SIDEWAYS → 400.

items.title: 8.7 Client failure contract
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: — (follows the review of 2026-10-24, DD-214)
  • Records: DD-214 (the review that scoped this; reserves CL-08); cites 8.4, ADR 055

items.title: Scope
items.text:
Test-completeness plus one minted rule: the review found the four client libraries test their happy path, their 4xx/5xx errors, and the connect-refused propagation — and test nothing about the responses in between. The systematic holes (DD-214): a 200 whose body fails the response model (no test proves what happens), a timeout (only connect-refused is proven), a token source that raises, and with_token under concurrency. This increment closes them across all four libraries:

  • aurelius-atlas-server-client — AdminApi, TypesApi, and get_lineage against garbage 200s; transport timeout; raising token source; concurrent wrappers on the shared pool.
  • aurelius-atlas-data2model-client — extract against garbage 200s; a 5xx carrying the Atlas body; timeout; raising token source.
  • aurelius-atlas-lineage-model-client — get against garbage 200s; timeout; raising token source; the 5xx/unreachable pair split into one test per behaviour, like the other three libraries.
  • aurelius-atlas-validate-entity-client — validate against garbage 200s; a 5xx carrying the Atlas body; timeout; raising token source.

It does not deliver: aux API tests (8.6), frontend error UX (7.19), container-stopping e2e (9.1), any production-code change — every test below pins behaviour the 8.4 clients already have (the review's core finding: the code is right, the proofs are missing).

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
CL-08 is minted here (DD-214's reservation): the behaviour exists in the 8.4 code (the model_validate_json calls) and was never stated. Everything else is already specified by the cited rule in 8.4; the bullets state the exact path each test pins.

Id Rule CL-08 A 2xx answer whose body the client's response model rejects — the wrong shape, a JSON type that is not the contract's, or bytes that are not JSON at all — raises the validation failure at the boundary: pydantic's ValidationError where the client parses bytes as its model, the JSON decoder's own error where it decodes first (the server client). Never the library's *ClientError (that is the non-2xx of CL-04) and never a success: a malformed success is the contract failing, and the caller's own recovery (LM-07's 502, the webapp's alert) is the app's job, exactly as with CL-05's transport failure.

Proven paths (stated in 8.4):

  • CL-04 (8.4): a non-2xx with a parseable Atlas body carries status, errorCode, and errorMessage in the library's *ClientError — proven today on 400/401/404; this increment adds the 5xx carrying the Atlas body (d2m, VE), the outage shape the 8.2 chain's breakers ride.
  • CL-05 (8.4): httpx.RequestError propagates as httpx's own error — proven today for ConnectError only; this increment adds the timeout (httpx.TimeoutException, the pool's own bound), the infrastructure failure category's client-lib half.
  • CL-03 (8.4): the token source is read per call — this increment adds the raising source: its error travels out unchanged and no request leaves (a caller whose credential fetch fails never speaks to the wire).
  • CL-03 / CL-02 (8.4): with_token shares the pool — this increment adds concurrency: two wrappers answering two callers at once, each bearer on its own request, one pool underneath.

No wire behaviour changes, so no Java/legacy citation is added.

items.title: 9.1 Targeted resilience e2e
items.text:
• Status: in progress
  • Pull request: — (follows the review of 2026-10-24, DD-214)
  • Records: RSL-01..03 (minted here); DD-214 (the review that scoped this); cites 7.7 (ALR-05), 7.3 (APC-05/10), 8.2/8.5 (LM-04, LM-12), DD-200, DD-206, DD-153, DD-173

items.title: Scope
items.text:
The review's last category (infra/technical failures, category 3) is proven today only in-process: 8.6 stops a fake transport, 8.5 opens fake breakers, the webapp alert chain is unit-tested with HttpTestingController. No test ever takes a real container down and watches the product answer. This increment adds the targeted outage suite — three scenarios, one per visible failure surface, each ≤ 2 minutes:

  • RSL-01 — the webapp's server outage, in a real browser: stop the atlas-server container of the running e2e stack, and the shell surfaces the outage the way ALR-05 promises (nginx 502 on /api → the bell's badge, the drawer's feed names the failed call); start the container and the app recovers without a reload — the next call succeeds and the panel answers (the alert stays in the feed: an outage is history, not amnesia).
  • RSL-02 — the lineage chain's upstream outage, across containers: stop the fixture Atlas of the 8.2 chain; the app's real httpx call hits a refused connection and the app answers the Atlas-shaped 502 (LM-12's container-side twin — 8.6 proved it in-process with a fake transport); start the fixture and the chain answers the canned graph again.
  • RSL-03 — the logout round-trip, in a real browser against the real Keycloak: sign in, log out from the navbar, and the IdP session ends — the app lands on the sign-in page (the guard's redirect, APC-05), and signing in again returns the greeted app. The SHC-05 logout path is unit-pinned in 7.19 (the fire-and-forget contract); this proves the Keycloak round-trip the unit can never run.

It does not deliver: chaos testing, sustained-outage behaviour, the circuit-breaker-open e2e (8.5's unit suite owns it; one outage event is one failure, and opening needs five), Elasticsearch-loss scenarios (the server spine's deferred backlog, DD-214), or any production-code change.

items.title: Rule definitions
items.text: Id Rule RSL-01 With the Atlas server down, the webapp surfaces the outage: an /api call that answers 5xx (nginx's 502) earns an error alert (ALR-05 chain), and when the server returns, the app recovers on the next call — no reload, no manual repair. RSL-02 With an upstream of the 8.2 chain down (fixture Atlas), the lineage-model app answers a request with the Atlas-shaped 502 (LM-12 over real transports, not a fake one), and recovers to the canned answer when the upstream returns. RSL-03 Logout ends the Keycloak session: after Logout, the app's routes answer with the sign-in redirect (APC-05), and signing in again lands the greeted app — the session round-trip is complete and repeatable.

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
• RSL-01 (7.7 ALR-05, 7.12): the alerts interceptor reports /api calls that fail with 5xx or status 0; a stopped container makes nginx answer 502 (its /api/ proxy resolves the upstream per request, DD-142 + the resolver pattern), so the browser's failed call follows the unit-tested path: bell badge, drawer feed row naming Request failed: GET /api/... 502. Recovery is the same stack's readiness probe (the conftest's version-endpoint poll, ATLAS_SERVER_HOST_PORT) after container.start().
  • RSL-02 (8.2 LM-04/05, 8.5 LM-12, DD-200): the app calls the fixture Atlas over the compose network; a stopped container answers connection refused, the app's httpx.RequestError handler answers the Atlas 502 body (errorCode ATLAS-500-00-001 family, DD-20's 8.x shape). The container handle is found by compose labels (the collector fixture's pattern, CIA-03 suite). Restart + the compose healthcheck (5s interval) restores the chain.
  • RSL-03 (SHC-05, APC-05/10, DD-153): Logout is the dropdown anchor (DD-153); keycloak.logout() ends the session at the IdP and returns to the app's origin. The root guard (APC-05, check-sso) then redirects to Keycloak's login — the same landing the authenticated fixture signs through — and the round-trip completes with the navbar greeting (SHC-05).

items.title: Java origin
items.text: No Java twin: Apache Atlas' webapp ships no resilience e2e (the legacy suite is integration-level, webapp/src/test). The scenarios follow the review (DD-214) category 3 and the Aurelius shell/chain rules cited above.

items.title: Deviations
items.text: None new. The outage answers ride the accepted 8.x shapes (DV-77's breaker 502, the SRV-04 error body) — cited, not restated.

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
E2E (Docker, real containers; budgets per scenario):

  • apps/aurelius-atlas-webapp/e2e/test__aurelius_atlas_webapp_resilience.py — new, runs after the main suite (filename order) so the outage touches only itself:
    • test__a_server_outage_surfaces_an_alert_and_the_app_recovers (RSL-01): stop the atlas-server container (fixture atlas_server_page_down, compose-label lookup like collector_container); poll /api/atlas/admin/version through nginx until 502 (≤ 60s — the nginx resolver's 10s cache); open the settings panel with the authenticated page; the bell badge dot is visible and the alerts drawer names the failed GET ... 502 (ALR-12 clears the dot on open); start the container, poll readiness; reopen the panel and the session answers (no alert added after the recovery). Budget: 120s + the session stack.
    • test__logout_returns_to_sign_in_and_signing_in_again_restores_the_app (RSL-03): authenticated page → hover the account dropdown → Logout; the page lands on Keycloak's login (the guard's redirect); sign in with the dev user; the navbar greets the identity again. Budget: 60s.
    • The outage fixture's finalizer always starts the container (a crashed test must not leave the dev stack down) and the resilience file owns the suite's only stop/start pair.
  • apps/aurelius-atlas-lineage-model/e2e/test__aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_resilience_e2e.py — new:
    • test__a_fixture_atlas_outage_answers_502_and_the_chain_recovers (@pytest.mark.covers("aurelius_atlas_lineage_model.app.create_app", "aurelius_atlas_lineage_model_client.client.LineageModelClient.get", rules=["RSL-02", "LM-12", "CL-30"])): the module fixture fixture_atlas_down stops the fixture-atlas container (compose-label lookup); api.get(E_IN) raises LineageModelClientError with status_code 502 and an Atlas error body whose errorCode the client parsed — a raw httpx GET /?guid= answers the identical body, proving the shape is the app's, not the client's; the test then starts the container and polls (≤ 90s) until api.get(E_IN) returns the canned extract again. Budget: 120s. The fixture's finalizer restarts the container as a crash-net so the scenarios file, which sorts after, always rides a live chain.
  • Gates: nx e2e aurelius-atlas-webapp -c ci and nx e2e aurelius-atlas-lineage-model -c ci green (the suites already gate in CI — these files join them); budgets are bounded by the in-test polls (deadline loops, no pytest-timeout dependency — it is not installed in this workspace), ≤ 2 min per scenario added. RSL-02 shows PASSED in the trace report (its marker); RSL-01/RSL-03 are Playwright-side, named in the docstrings (ADR 049's frontend convention — the gap baseline grows by exactly those two, the webapp rule-id family).
  • Lint: ruff clean on both files; no .env/compose changes (the fixed ports 18444/18445 already exist; the chain's fixture needs no host port — the outage is observed through the app's own published answer).

items.title: Specification Template
items.text:
Copy the block below into N-M-short-slug.md and fill it in before writing code.

# N.M Increment title

- **Status:** planned | in progress | in review | done
- **Pull request:** link
- **Records:** ADR / DD numbers this increment adds or relies on

## Scope

What this increment delivers: endpoints, operations, projects. Then what it explicitly does not
deliver, with the increment that will.

## Semantics

Each rule the behaviour must obey, in plain words, with an id that tests name in
`@pytest.mark.covers(..., rules=["XXX-NN"])`.

| Id     | Rule |
| ------ | ---- |
| XXX-01 |      |

## Java origin

The Atlas classes (2.4.0) whose behaviour this ports, so reviewers can compare.

## Deviations

Deliberate differences from Apache Atlas, each added to [Deviations](../deviations.md).

## Acceptance

The parity scenarios and test files that prove the rules, and how to run them.

items.title: Data Governance
items.text:
Governance in the terms the business uses: people discover and understand data, know who is accountable for it, see how it flows and how sensitive it is, and can prove all of it. Concretely, that is how Aurelius Atlas describes, classifies, connects, and accounts for data — the catalogue's own subject: the type system, lineage, glossary, classifications, and audit trail. The rules live in the increment semantics specs; these pages assemble them into the governance view.

Page Scope Written by Roles & Responsibilities Who owns and who may act: authorizer roles, dataset ownership 6.2 (ADR 042) Data Dictionary The type system as the catalogue's dictionary: typedefs, built-in models, inheritance 1.6 (material exists from 1.1–1.5) Data Quality Glossary, terms, business metadata, labels as quality signals 5.2, 5.3 Data Lineage Processes, inputs/outputs, depth and direction, on-demand lineage 5.1 Compliance & Auditability Entity audit events, classifications with validity, audit REST 3.5, 6.2 Every page here is Planned — where do I read the rules?

items.title: Data Storage
items.text:
All catalogue data lives in one search store — the system of record and the search index at once (ADR 047). There is no graph database, relational store, or separate index to keep in step. The current implementation is Elasticsearch 9, reached through the store library; its knobs and mechanics are in the store's design documentation.

Why is one store the only store?

Catalogue data answers five verbs — write, read, search, traverse, classify — and ADR 047 graded each candidate arrangement by them: every extra store adds a second place where the same facts must agree, plus its own backup, upgrade, and monitoring. One store that serves all five verbs turns consistency into a single-writer problem and self-hosting into running one service and one store.

items.title: The store today (increments 0.2, 1.4)
items.text:
The store library owns the client: the link is TLS-only with certificate verification and credentials — an unencrypted endpoint is rejected at settings validation, before the service opens. A deployment runs and monitors the cluster; the development arrangement runs one (dev/elasticsearch).

Type definitions move as one unit of storage: the store replaces all definitions whole under a concurrency guard, so a change to several definitions lands atomically, with one version number for all types (DD-028). This is a property the type system needs — Atlas changes several definitions in one transaction, a create stores all of a request or none — stated here, implemented there: the alias names, write-index mechanics, and size trade-offs are the design documentation's. The unit loads into the type registry when the service starts (rule TDS-12). The definitions are not searched — searching over catalogue entries arrives with search in increment 4.1.

items.title: The entity layout (increment 2.2)
items.text:
Every catalogue entry (an entity of any type) is one record, found by its identifier: a random UUID, as Atlas's clients already know it (DD-044). A read by identifier always sees the last write; nothing waits for the search index to catch up (DD-043). Attribute values are kept with their exact digits and become searchable when search arrives (4.1). A value that is a structure is kept inside its entry; a link to another entry is kept as that entry's identifier, so a renamed entry is never shown under its old name (DD-049). Each entry also lists, searchably, the identifiers of the entries it links to, so that deleting an entry finds the entries that link to it (DD-057). A deleted entry is kept, marked deleted, until it is purged; a purge or a hard delete removes it within the same all-or-nothing write as everything else the request changes (DD-056).

The store gives the catalogue the three guarantees its graph database gave Atlas, each recorded:

  • A unique value is held once per type. Two entries of one type cannot share a qualifiedName, even when two servers try at the same instant; a deleted entry gives its value up (DD-045).
  • A write of several entries succeeds or fails as a whole, also when a server dies part-way: a journal lets the next start undo what was left half done. While a write is in flight another reader may see part of it (DD-046, DV-16).
  • Concurrent changes are detected, not lost. A change is written only over the version it was read in (DD-047).

The concrete indices, mappings and write steps are the core library's design documentation.

items.title: Rules that bind storage
items.text:
• Schema changes go by recorded migration, data moved rather than replaced (ADR 023).
  • Data has a stated lifetime the system enforces; purged data is gone (ADR 025, delete semantics in 2.5).
  • Recovery is from a named snapshot (ADR 026, snapshots in 6.4).
  • Encryption in transit is TLS with verification (data encryption); at rest belongs to the deployment.

items.title: Platform
items.text:
How the Aurelius Atlas system is connected, delivered, observed, kept alive, and secured. Content arrives with the increments listed per page; see the tree convention on the Architecture page.

Page Scope Written by Components & Interfaces The running parts by role: service, dashboards, store, identity, signals, with one anchor line written (0.2–0.6) Data Pipelines The catalogue's flows: request → store, model load at start-up; no streaming plane (ADR 050) 2.4 Tree Subject Written by Connectivity REST contract, TLS, service-to-service links 0.5 → 6.1 Delivery Configuration, change, testing, release, deployment 0.3 → 6.4 Observability Metrics, logs, traces, alerts 6.4 (dev stack exists today) Resilience Availability posture, incidents, snapshots, recovery 6.4 Security Identity, access, secrets, encryption 0.1 → 6.2

items.title: Components & Interfaces
items.text:
The parts of the running system (increments 0.2–0.6 today) and the interfaces between them. The production shape is this same set — one service, one store, one identity provider, one signal path — with the deployment supplying certificates and endpoints. The development arrangement mirrors it; where a row describes development, that is labelled.

graph LR
    B[Browser] -->|HTTPS: REST| S[Catalogue service]
    S -->|TLS + credentials| E[(Search store)]
    S -->|TLS| O[Signal collector]
    B -->|OIDC| K[Identity provider]
    K -->|TLS| P[(Provider database)]
    O --> G[Signal backends]

The catalogue serves browsers and the store serves the catalogue; identity and observation sit beside the path, not on it.

Current implementations. The catalogue service is a FastAPI app (aurelius-atlas-server), serving on Atlas's own port; the dashboards are the vendored Atlas dashboardv2/dashboardv3, built from 2.4.0 source; the search store is Elasticsearch 9, reached through aurelius-atlas-store-es; the identity provider is Keycloak, on its own Postgres; the collector and the signal backends are an OpenTelemetry Collector with Prometheus, Tempo, Loki, and Grafana (dev/observability).

Where is the event plane?

Atlas integrations hook a Kafka stream: hook messages in, change notifications out. The catalogue carries no streaming plane — the template's event slice was removed (ADR 050, DV-01) — so every integration is a REST call, and the catalogue's change events are its own store records (audit events arrive with increment 3.5).

Part Role Contract it offers Catalogue service The catalogue's API — Atlas 2.4.0's REST contract; owns the store's lifetime at start-up HTTPS; configured only through its environment (ADR 018) Dashboards The Atlas UI, served by the catalogue service from the API's origin Static files; the API takes precedence (DD-018) Search store The only store: system of record and search index at once (ADR 047) TLS with certificate verification and credentials Identity provider The shared sign-in for every authenticated surface (ADR 007); the examples use it today, the API from 6.1 OIDC over verified TLS Provider database The identity provider's own store, and the template examples' — not the catalogue's (ADR 047) TLS with full verification Signal collector The single collection point for the system's signals (ADR 034) Signals leave the system only through it; a deployment points the exporter at its own collector

No endpoint needs a login yet

The identity provider signs people in today for the template examples, but the API accepts anonymous calls and the session reports no user, groups, or permissions. Authentication arrives with increment 6.1; the difference is recorded as DV-04 until then.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text:
The REST contract is Atlas 2.4.0's, proven by parity scenarios (ADR 046, ADR 052). The service–store interface is the store library, https-only. Signals leave only through the collector (ADR 034). Every service-to-service path is TLS with CA verification (data encryption). The endpoint names, ports, and settings of each path belong to the parts themselves: the server's knobs are in its design documentation, the store's in its library's.

TLS material is per project — declared, issued, and cleaned per project, development material only (TLS Certificates). A deployment serves with its own certificates.

Planned

items.title: Connectivity
items.text:
How Aurelius Atlas talks to its clients and services: the REST contract, TLS, and service-to-service links.

Page Scope Written by Integration Methods REST v2 API and dashboard surfaces; no streams (ADR 050) written (0.5); resources with 1.6 API Management The Atlas public contract, versioning, error body, OpenAPI written (0.5) Networking Production requirements (TLS, DNS names); dev compose topology after written (0.2/0.6)

items.title: API Management
items.text: The API Aurelius Atlas exposes is Apache Atlas 2.4.0's REST API — the product's public contract, kept while its implementation is replaced (ADR 046).

items.title: The contract
items.text:
• Base path /api/atlas/v2/..., same resource families as Atlas (admin, types, entity, …), added increment by increment per the roadmap.
  • Wire format is Atlas's, including its normalisations: the server's default response class is the Atlas JSON media type, and error bodies follow Atlas's AtlasErrorCode (status, code, message template) via AtlasError — the enum members are copied from Java Atlas, not invented.
  • No OpenAPI surface is served: the contract is the wire format itself, specified by parity scenarios whose expectations are read from the Atlas 2.4.0 source and its own tests, each citing where (ADR 052).
Why is there no OpenAPI / Swagger UI?

Atlas ships a Swagger description and integrators expect one. The description would be a second, hand-maintained statement of a contract that parity scenarios already pin byte-for-byte — and the two drifting apart is the failure ADR 030 exists to prevent. The scenarios, not a schema, are the authority (ADR 030).

items.title: Change policy
items.text:
A REST-visible difference is a decision, not an edit

Code that answers differently than Atlas 2.4.0 without a deviation entry is a defect, not a simplification: the parity report links every tolerated difference to its entry, and the client-facing contract is ADR 046's to keep.

A difference that is kept is recorded in deviations with the rule id that changed, and the parity scenario carries a deviations entry naming it. Shared concepts change only compatibly (ADR 017); the version number of the contract stays Atlas 2.4.0's for the life of the conversion.

items.title: Integration Methods
items.text:
How clients integrate with Aurelius Atlas: request/response over the Atlas REST API, served to browsers and machines alike. The catalogue has no streaming plane — the event-streaming slice of the template was removed (ADR 050), so every integration is a call, and the catalogue's change events are its own store records (audit events arrive with increment 3.5), not a feed.

Atlas published change events to Kafka — where are they?

Nowhere, by decision: the event-streaming slice was removed with ADR 050 and the Kafka hooks are recorded as DV-01. Integrations that watched the feed poll the REST API instead; the catalogue's own audit records (increment 3.5) are the durable event history.

items.title: Surfaces
items.text: Three surfaces, one origin: the REST API for machines, the dashboards for people (the Atlas UI, served by the catalogue service from the API's origin — DD-018), and the admin endpoints for liveness, readiness, and status. Which endpoints answer today, and what each returns, is the server's own documentation: aurelius-atlas-server and its project README.md. Every one is byte-for-byte Atlas's in body and status, proven by parity scenarios (ADR 052); where Aurelius Atlas must answer differently, the difference is a recorded deviation, never a silent one.

items.title: By phase
items.text: The roadmap adds the Atlas resource families in order: types (1.6), entity read/write and delete (2.3–2.5), relationships and classifications (3.x), search and the Atlas DSL (4.x), lineage and glossary (5.x), authentication and authorization (6.1–6.2), import and export of Atlas migration archives (6.3). Each arrives with parity scenarios and, where behaviour differs, a recorded deviation — clients integrate against the contract described in API Management, not against this page.

items.title: Networking
items.text: How the parts reach each other. The page states what the system requires of a network; the development topology that satisfies them, slice by slice, is the contributor guide's Dev Topology.

items.title: Production
items.text:
The production topology is the deployment arrangement's subject — deployment (6.4). What the system requires of it:

  • Every path TLS with certificate verification against the deployment's own CA (data encryption). The plaintext listeners developers see exist only in the development arrangement, as named relaxations.
  • Discovery by DNS name, with the service names present in the certificates. Services reach each other by name, not IP — verification is of the name in the certificate, so an address that connects can still be rejected.
  • The catalogue service reaches the store and the signal collector; browsers reach the catalogue service for the API and the UI, and the identity provider for sign-in. Nothing else needs a path: the store serves only the catalogue service, and the collector receives signals without the system calling back through it. Reaching the collector's ingest ports is not enough to write to them — the browser leg accepts only Keycloak user tokens, the service leg only the shared ingest token (DD-193).

items.title: Development and CI
items.text:
The development arrangement is one compose project per infrastructure slice, each on its own network, with the app's containers joining the networks of the slices they use — so the service-name rule above is exercised locally, exactly as a deployment must satisfy it. The published host ports, network names, and per-slice commands are in Dev Topology and each slice's README; certificates are development material issued per project (TLS Certificates).

The store is reachable only by service name

Pointing a client at localhost or an IP address — the reflex from a laptop install — fails certificate verification, not connectivity: the store's certificate is issued for its service name. Join the slice's compose network and use the name, as the server's e2e container does.

items.title: Delivery
items.text:
How changes reach production: configuration, change control, testing, release, and deployment. Parts of this tree are already written (Change Management, Testing); the rest is filled per the map below.

Page Scope Written by Configuration Management Production env-var contract (ADR 018); dev/CI secrets and prefixes written (0.5) Change Management Release → acceptance/production hand-over (ADR 024); dev + pipeline after — Testing Layer map, CI gate (production bar); developer-side conventions after — Test Suite Review Dated review of every suite: coverage + non-happy-flow representativeness, hardening increments (DD-214) written (2026-10) Release Management One versioned whole (ADR 019): version, inventory, signing, promotion written (0.1) Deployment Image-per-service, compose layouts, promote-by-declared-path (ADR 024) 6.4

items.title: Change Management
items.text:
Every change reaches production the same way: it merges into main only after the pipeline proves it, ships inside a signed release, and is then promoted by the deployment that receives it. This page describes the released version and what a deployment receives first, then the development flow that produces them — the order a reader of the running system needs.

The environments the system itself operates are two: development, which is each person's own machine, and test, which is the pipeline. Acceptance and production are not operated by the system; they exist per engagement, and the release hands over an artifact complete enough for a deployment to promote from. The reasoning behind that split is recorded in ADR 024.

Where are acceptance and production, then?

Outside this system's boundary, by design. The system's obligation to them ends at the hand-over — a signed, self-contained artifact — and each engagement runs its own promotion path from there (The hand-over obligation).

items.title: Release
items.text: A version of the system is released as one versioned whole: one number, one changelog, and one release event that publishes every deployable part together as signed, provenance-bearing artifacts. Passing the test environment is what qualifies a change to be part of a release.

items.title: Acceptance and Production
items.text: What happens to a released version beyond the pipeline is decided per project or customer: acceptance and production are where an engagement's own requirements live — who signs off, on what environment, under what schedule.

items.title: The hand-over obligation
items.text:
The system's obligation to those environments is the hand-over. A release hands over an artifact that is:

  • signed and versioned, so the deployment can prove what it received;
  • configured only through the settings the environment supplies;
  • promotable and rollable back without knowledge that lives only with the people who built it.

A project that wants promotion to acceptance and production to be a declared, repeatable path writes that path against the released artifacts, as part of its own deployment arrangement.

items.title: Development and the pipeline
items.text: Where changes are made and proven before the releases above: each person's own machine, and the pipeline that gates the merge.

items.title: Development
items.text:
The dev container

Each developer works in their own dev container — an isolated environment with the tools, dependencies, and the whole system (application and its infrastructure) running on the developer's machine, keeping experiments away from everyone else's work. The container is itself a versioned artifact (ADR 011); setup is in the Development Environment guide.

Developers commit to a feature branch in the version-control repository, created from main. The branch isolates the changes until they are ready for review and testing.

items.title: Test
items.text:
The test environment is the pipeline: every change is validated there before it merges into main. The pipeline runs the same checks as the local hooks, and then the full suite — the layers are listed in Testing:

  • Code quality — formatting, linting, typing, secret scanning.
  • Unit tests — each module in isolation.
  • Parity scenarios — REST behaviour checked against Apache Atlas 2.4.0, with every expectation cited from the Atlas source (ADR 052).
  • End-to-end tests — the built image against real services, not substitutes (ADR 012).

When the automated tests pass, the feature branch is ready for review: one reviewer confirms independent understanding, and the change merges with two human signatures (ADR 044).

A green pipeline is necessary, not sufficient

The pipeline proves the change works; two humans sign that it is right — the task owner, who can explain the change, and one reviewer, who confirms independent understanding. A merge with green checks and one signature is a process violation, not a shortcut (ADR 043 keeps AI review advisory for the same reason).

items.title: Configuration Management
items.text: Settings arrive at start-up through one channel and fail loudly (ADR 018). The contract is the same everywhere; what differs is who supplies the values. Production is first below, and the development and CI arrangements come after.

items.title: Production
items.text:
The unit that ships is the container image (release management). Its configuration is the environment, read once at start-up into a frozen settings object — no library reads the environment afterwards, and apps pass settings objects down. Validation failures (missing key, bad scheme, half a TLS pair) stop start-up with a message naming the variable, so a misconfigured deployment never serves traffic.

What a deployment must supply has no defaults — the service does not start without it (SRV-01, SRV-02): the store's endpoints and credentials, and the CA that signs the store's certificate. Where those values come from — an orchestrator secret store, certificate provisioning — is the deployment page's subject (6.4). The knobs are named, with defaults and validation, in the server's design documentation: Configuration.

A half TLS pair stops the server from starting

The serving certificate and key are a pair: both set, or both unset — enforced at start-up. A container that mounts only the certificate exits with a message naming the missing variable; this is the design working, not a broken image.

Naming. App-owned settings carry a per-project prefix, so two projects in one workspace can never read each other's values. Keys that third-party code (the platform's, the observability exporter's, infrastructure images) reads must stay bare to be read at all — the prefix list lives in the root AGENTS.md.

Why do the variable names carry such long prefixes?

One project's environment leaks into all of that project's tasks, so a bare PORT set by the frontend example would be visible to the server's tests. The prefix is what keeps two projects' settings from shadowing each other; keys the ecosystem's own images read must stay bare to be read at all.

items.title: Development and CI
items.text:
The same channel, with repository-local plumbing: each project's plaintext .env carries dev defaults, and its real settings travel with the code as ciphertext (ADR 008). The rules that keep the two in step — decryption as a task dependency, ciphertext as the source of truth, TLS material as configuration — are the secrets guide's, with the commands: Secrets Management.

Editing .env alone is undone by the next CI run

Ciphertext is the source of truth and plaintext is generated from it. An .env edit that is not re-encrypted disappears the moment CI decrypts — the change works locally and fails in the pipeline, with the plaintext file as the only visible symptom.

items.title: Release Management
items.text: The system releases as one versioned whole (ADR 019): one version number across the workspace, one changelog, one release event.

items.title: The flow
items.text:
graph LR
    C[Commits] -->|version| V[Version + changelog]
    V --> B[Image + inventory]
    B -->|scan green| SG[Signed + published]
    SG -->|promote by declared path| P[Production]

The unit that passes validation is the unit that ships, and a deployment promotes the signed artifact along the declared path (ADR 010, ADR 024).

  1. Version — the release tool reads conventional commits and bumps the workspace as one: one version, the project versions, and the changelog. A candidate can be cut locally for testing without publishing anything.
  2. Build — every part produces its wheel and its image; the validated unit is the unit that ships (ADR 010).
  3. Inventory — images carry a contents inventory (ADR 033) and a vulnerability scan runs over the affected images in CI.
  4. Sign and publish — published artifacts are signed with provable origin (ADR 029); the publish pipeline promotes a validated release along the declared path (ADR 024).
  5. Docs — the site publishes per release tag (publishing).

The commands — the candidate cut, the publish, the docs site mechanics — are the contributor guide's: Releasing.

items.title: Conventions that make one-version work
items.text:
Conventional commit titles are required (the changelog is generated from them); template updates merge from the template remote without versioning pressure because the repo keeps its history (ADR 050's mergeability requirement). The runtime version window is declared, not floating (ADR 031).

A non-conventional commit title poisons the changelog

The changelog is generated, so its entries are only as good as the titles: a commit titled "fixes" contributes "fixes". feat:/fix: also drive the version bump — a miscategorised title releases a minor where a patch was meant, and the one-version rule makes that number every part's number.

items.title: Test Suite Review (2026-10-24)
items.text:
A workspace-wide review of every test suite: coverage, and — the part a coverage number cannot show — representativeness: do the tests cover the non-happy flows as well as the happy ones? The methodology and the layers are Testing; this page records what the review found and what it committed to build next (DD-214).

Coverage is reported to SonarQube, whose quality gate is the enforcement (Testing step 6). This page carries measured baselines as reference figures, not as gates: the Python apps' from their generated coverage.xml, the frontend's from the lcov.info files under coverage/. The Python libraries' coverage is generated in CI only, so their figures live in Sonar, not here.

The pattern: infrastructure failures are a strength (lineage-model, store-es, auth set the house style — fakes with recording seams, breakers proven through the management API). The systematic holes are: mid-request infra failures (server, core), business-rule states in the frontend (session lifecycle, RBAC-driven UI as 6.x lands), interrupted/async states (timeouts, out-of-order responses, concurrent callers), and the client libraries' response-shape failures (2xx-with-garbage, timeout vs connect error).

items.title: Deferred backlog (ranked)
items.text:
The review's priority was the frontend, the auxiliary APIs, and the client libraries. These findings are ranked backlog, not drops:

  1. Server spine — store failure mid-request (surface as an Atlas-body 500, pin the parity of Java's behaviour; test routes/types.py against a raising TypedefStore, plus typedef_store refresh failure and concurrent POST /typedefs). Natural fit for the 2.x instance-store track.
  2. core — ES transport/ApiError propagation on ElasticsearchTypedefDocument.read/write; two concurrent _change callers on one store.
  3. store-es — request_timeout elapsing → TransportError; double-open race; _major of a -SNAPSHOT version.
  4. auth — circuit recovery (half-open → closed), JWKS TTL expiry, malformed discovery/JWKS documents.
  5. otel — concurrent bearer() mint under the lock; mint responses missing access_token/expires_in.
  6. parity — the transport raising mid-scenario.
  7. dashboard — stays as-is by policy; the server e2e is its net.
  8. Storybook gate — test-storybook runs 73 stories as real Playwright tests but is opt-in; wiring it into the PR gate is an open call.

items.text:
Template code stays out of the hardening scope (the trace check already excludes it; this review confirms the exemption):

  • aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example — the template's example app; broad tests already, no parity contract, not trace-checked.
  • aurelius-atlas-sdk's aws.py, msal.py, logger.py and aurelius-atlas-example — template starting points (ADR 050 removed the slices that used them).
  • aurelius-atlas-dashboard — vendored Apache Atlas source (DD-017); its regression net is the server e2e, by policy.

items.title: Reading the numbers
items.text:
• App figures: coverage.xml as regenerated by nx test <app> -c ci (2026-10-24 run). Line coverage only — the Sonar gate also weighs new-code coverage, which is where a hardening PR is measured.
  • Frontend figures: coverage/<project>/lcov-report from the Vitest runs; the webapp aggregate includes imported lib sources it never exercises — its own directories sit at 95–100%.
  • Test counts drift with every increment; the trace report (uv run aurelius-atlas-trace report) is the live system of record for rule/function coverage.

items.title: Testing Strategy
items.text: This page states how Aurelius Atlas is tested: the layers the gate stands on, and what each proves. The gate itself is defined once and runs everywhere (ADR 014) — the same checks locally and in CI. The commands, file conventions, and failure triage are the contributor guide's: Testing. The merge bar for conversion work is the Definition of Done in the conversion roadmap.

items.title: The layers
items.text:
Layer What it proves Unit Functions and modules in isolation, milliseconds-fast, offline; the store is a stand-in client Parity scenarios REST behaviour equals Apache Atlas 2.4.0 — expectations read from its source and its own tests, each citing where (ADR 052) Naming convention Every public function and every specified rule id is named by a test marker, as a review pointer — not a gate (ADR 056) E2E (backend) The built image against real services over TLS (ADR 010, ADR 012) E2E (frontend) Critical user flows through the real browser stack Visual Visual regressions of the shared UI library — template slice, leaves with it (DD-019)

Python units are milliseconds and offline-safe; e2e is the shipped artifact against real services — never mocks of the things being shipped. Parity is the layer the conversion adds: a scenario states the request and the response Atlas gives, and a visible difference is a recorded deviation, not a silent test change. Inside every layer, tests are written in the Arrange-Act-Assert shape — set the world up, run the thing, check the result — with behavior-oriented names and reusable fixtures in place of copy-pasted setup (AAA).

The current stack, named once as evidence: pytest with pytest-cov and pytest-mock for the Python layers, Testcontainers to bring the real services up under E2E, Playwright for the browser flows, Vitest for the Angular side, Storybook with Chromatic for the visual layer, all orchestrated by Nx.

A stand-in store client in units, a real store in e2e — why both?

They prove different things at different costs. The stand-in keeps unit tests millisecond-fast and offline so a developer runs them constantly; the store integration itself — the part most likely to break against a real server — is proven where the unit of validation is the unit that ships: the built image against real services over TLS (ADR 010, ADR 012).

items.title: The CI gate
items.text:
The gate is what protects production: no change reaches main — and nothing is released — without it. The stages, in the order they run:

  1. Quality — formatting, linting, markdown, secret scanning.
  2. Test + E2E — the affected projects, secrets decrypted first, images built, real services started. The executed results are the evidence: a change merges when its tests pass (ADR 056).
  3. Artifact + inventory + scan — the image, its contents inventory (ADR 033), a vulnerability scan.
  4. Analysis — code quality and security of the affected projects.

Merge requires all affected stages green; the test results and coverage are what reviewers read. The pipeline definition is in the repository's CI configuration.

Coverage is measured in every -c ci test run and uploaded to the analysis stage: SonarQube receives each project's coverage.xml / lcov.info, and its quality gate is the coverage gate — there is deliberately no second coverage flag in the pipeline. The last full review of what the suites prove — coverage baselines and non-happy-flow representativeness per project — is the Test Suite Review (DD-214).

items.title: Indicators
items.text:
The gate aims at delivery outcomes, not coverage for its own sake. The indicators follow the DORA metrics, with starting-point targets to be operationalized with business stakeholders:

Indicator Direction Starting target Intent Change failure rate Down < 15% Less release risk, more confidence in delivery. Mean time to restore Down < 1 hour Less customer impact when a failure occurs. Lead time for changes Down < 7 days Predictable delivery from development to live.

Each is measured from the system's own records: the failure rate from deployment logs and incident tracking, the restore time from detection to restoration in the incident record, the lead time from commit to deployment in the pipeline's metadata. Leading signals watch for trouble before users do: gate pass rates, the flaky-test rate and how quickly flakes are fixed, recurring regressions, execution time per layer, coverage of critical paths, and the share of changes that carry test updates.

Flaky tests are fixed, never skipped

A skipped test silently deletes the evidence the gate is made of: the report reads as green while the behaviour it stood for goes unproven. Retrying a flaky test hides its root cause — timing, isolation, shared environment — which is the bug worth fixing.

items.title: Data Encryption
items.text: This page answers where data is encrypted, from the data-protection record (ADR 039). Whether a path is protected is answered from configuration, not by probing a running system (that record's R5) — this page names the rule per path; where each knob lives is in the component's design documentation.

items.title: In transit (production)
items.text:
Every path data travels on inside the system is TLS with certificate verification, by role:

Path Rule Browser → catalogue service TLS with the deployment's own certificate; the E2E suite proves the served image over TLS Service → search store TLS only — plain endpoints are rejected by settings validation, before connecting Service → relational store (examples only) TLS with full verification; the catalogue spine has no relational store (ADR 047) Service → signal collector TLS; exporters trust the deployment's CA; the service leg (gRPC/HTTP) demands the shared ingest token (bearer), the browser leg demands the user's own Keycloak token, passed through the proxy untouched (DD-193) Service → identity provider (token verify) TLS issuer with CA trust in CI/E2E; the local browser path is the named relaxation below

The knobs that make each row true — the setting names, verification flags, and trust material per component — live in the components' design documentation (server, store).

items.title: Proven in development and CI
items.text: The posture is tested, not just configured: the store library rejects plain endpoints; the dev store serves TLS only and is health-checked over it; the server's e2e runs the built image over HTTPS against that store; the template examples' relational-store containers start with TLS-only client authentication and connect with full verification. The per-command proofs are in the slice READMEs under dev/ and each project's e2e/.

items.title: At rest
items.text: Encryption at rest is owned by the stores and is not configured in this repository; deployments choose store-level encryption (disk or volume encryption). Development data is throwaway and carries no at-rest guarantee — the arrangement states this rather than implying it.

items.title: Named relaxation (development arrangement only)
items.text:
Plaintext exists only in the development arrangement, each occurrence deliberate: a browser-facing dev convenience listener on the identity provider, plaintext developer-only surfaces on a developer machine, and the E2E browser navigating with certificate verification skipped — every one of them recorded, with its reason, its out-of-band verification, and the commands around it, in TLS Certificates.

A deployment replicates the posture, not the conveniences

Every production path is verified TLS. The plaintext listeners are development material with named reasons, commented in the repository at each occurrence, citing ADR 039 — they never travel to a deployment.
